statement: A $5-$card hand is called a three-of-a-kind if it consists of $3$ cards of one rank and $2$ cards of two other distinct ranks. To the nearest ten-thousandth, find the probability that a random $5$ card hand drawn from a standard deck of cards is a three-of-a-kind.
solution:
To have a three-of-a-kind, you must pick the rank for which $3$ suits are drawn, pick the two ranks that have $1$ suit drawn, and also pick the suits drawn. The total number of $5$ card hands that can be drawn from a standard deck is $\binom{52}{5}$, as the order of the cards drawn is irrelevant. 

$$$$

We must determine the number of ways to draw the three-of-a-kind hand. There are $13$ ways to pick the rank that will have $3$ of its suits drawn out. Once the rank is selected, there are $\binom{4}{3}$ ways to pick the three suits of that rank that are selected, as the order of those suits being selected is irrelevant. Once those are picked, we need to select two more cards of two distinct suits. There are $\binom{12}{2}$ ways to pick the two ranks of cards that will occupy our last two spots, as the order of their selection is irrelevant. Once we have selected the two ranks, there are $4$ suits of each of those ranks to select from, so we multiply by $4^2$ to account for the number of ways to pick the suits. By the mulitplication principle, the number of three-of-a-kind hands is $$13\cdot\binom{4}{3}\binom{12}{2}\cdot 4^2$$ Therefore, the probability of a three-of-a-kind is $$\dfrac{13\cdot\binom{4}{3}\binom{12}{2}\cdot 4^2}{\binom{52}{5}}\approx 0.0211$$
hints: To have a three-of-a-kind, you must pick the rank for which $3$ suits are drawn, pick the two ranks that have $1$ suit drawn, and also pick the suits drawn.

title: Binary Strings
statement: A binary string of length $n$ is a string of $n$ characters that are each $0$ or $1$. Find the number of binary strings of length $n$ that either begin with $1$ or end with $00$. Report the answer for $n = 10$.
solution:
There are a couple approaches that can be taken here. This question is looking to count events where either one event or another happens, and those events are not disjoint. Thus, one should either work with the complement or use inclusion-exclusion. In this case, both of them work, and the easier one is complementation, as you can visualize it on the blanks directly.

$$$$

The complement of the event in question is that the string must begin with $0$ and not end with $00$. The rest of the string is unrestricted. Therefore, there is only $1$ option for the first spot, and there are three options for the last two spots: $01, 10,$ or $11$. In the other $n-3$ spots, there are no restrictions, so there are $2$ options for each of those $n-3$ spots. Therefore, the total number of strings in the complement is $1 \cdot 2^{n-3} \cdot 3$, where the $1$ is the first spot, $2^{n-3}$ is the middle $n-3$ spots that are not restricted, and the $3$ is for the last two spots. Thus, the number strings where the string starts with $1$ or ends with $00$ is $2^n - 3 \cdot 2^{n-3}$, as there are $2^n$ total strings of length $n$ ($0$ or $1$ for each of $n$ spots). With $n = 10$, the answer is $1024 - 384 = 640$.
hints: The complement is that the string must begin with $0$ and not end with $00$. The rest of the string is unrestricted.

title: Poisson PGF
statement: For non-negative integer-valued random variables $X$, one defines the $\textit{probability generating function}$ (PGF) of $X$ by $p_X(z) = E[z^X]$ for $|z| \leq 1$. Find the PGF $p_X(z)$ of $X \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ with $\lambda = 2$ and report the value of $p_X(1/2)$ to the nearest thousandth..
solution: There doesn't appear to be a very easy way to compute this expectation normally, so using LOTUS is a good starting point whenever all other methods don't seem tractable. We have that $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, so $\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}$ for each integer $k \geq 0$. Therefore, we have that $$p_X(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^X] = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda} \cdot z^k = e^{-\lambda} \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(\lambda z)^k}{k!}$$ by LOTUS and some simplification. Now note that the summation remaining is just the Maclaurin series for $f(x) = e^x$ evaluated at $\lambda z$. Therefore, the sum above is just $e^{\lambda z}$. Substituting into the above, we have that $p_X(z) = e^{-\lambda} \cdot e^{\lambda z} = e^{\lambda(z-1)}$. With the specified values, we have that the answer is $e^{-1}$.
hints: There doesn't appear to be a very easy way to compute this expectation normally, so using LOTUS is a good starting point.

title: Binomial PGF
statement: For non-negative integer-valued random variables $X$, one defines the probability generating function (PGF) of $X$ by $p_X(z) = E[z^X]$ for $|z| \leq 1$. Find the PGF $p_X(z)$ of $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ with $n = 5, p = 1/2$, and report the value of $p_X(1/2)$.
solution: There doesn't appear to be a very easy way to compute this expectation normally, so using LOTUS is a good starting point. Since $X \sim \text{Binom}(n,p)$, $\mathbb{P}[X = k] = \displaystyle \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ for $k = 0,1,\dots, n$. The LOTUS sum is given by $$p_X(z) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}[X=k]z^k = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \displaystyle \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} \cdot z^k = \sum_{k=0}^n \displaystyle \binom{n}{k}(pz)^k(1-p)^{n-k}$$ The upper index lowers to $n$ because $\mathbb{P}[X = k] = 0$ for $k > n$. The last sum can be evaluated by application of the Binomial Theorem with $a = pz$ and $b = 1-p$. Therefore, it evaluates to $(pz + (1-p))^n$, and this is the PGF of $X$. With the specific values, this evaluates to $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^5 = \dfrac{243}{1024}$.
hints: There doesn't appear to be a very easy way to compute this expectation normally, so using LOTUS is a good starting point.

title: Quick Blue
statement: A bowl has $3$ red and $4$ blue marbles inside. The marbles are drawn out one-by-one until without replacement. Find the probability that it takes more than $5$ draws to draw out the last blue marble.
solution:
For all $4$ blue marbles to be removed within the first $5$ draws, there must be exactly $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws. We know that there is at least $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws no matter what, as there are only $4$ blue marbles total. If there were at least $2$ red marbles in the first $5$ draws, there could only be at most $3$ blue marbles in the first $5$ draws, meaning that the last blue marble would be outside of the first $5$ draws. Therefore, the only time that all $4$ blue marbles are removed in the first $5$ draws is if there is exactly $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws. In other words, the last two draws must both be red. 

$$$$

Since sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process, the probability that the last two marbles drawn are red is the same as the probability that the first two are red. The probability that the first marble drawn is red is $\frac{3}{7}$, as $3$ of the $7$ marbles at the start are the red. Afterwards, the probability that the second marble is red is $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$, as there would be $2$ red marbles left out of $6$ total. Multiplying these together, the probability that the last two marbles are red is $\frac{3}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{7}$. This implies that the probability that all $4$ blue marbles are drawn out in the first $5$ turns is $\frac{1}{7}$, meaning the probability that it takes more than $5$ turns is $1 - 1/7 = 6/7$.
hints: What must be true for all $4$ blue marbles to be removed within the first $5$ draws?

title: Multicoin I
statement: $n \geq 2$ people labelled $1-n$ play a game where player $1$ starts with a coin that has probability $0 < p < 1$ of showing heads per flip. The first player to flip a head wins. If player $i$ lands a tails, then they pass the coin to player $i+1$ for their turn to flip. Once the coin reaches player $n$, the coin circles back around to the start for player $1$ to flip again, and the cycle repeats. Find the probability that player $1$ wins when $n = 5$ and $p = 1/3$.
solution:
The probability here is very dependent on what happens at the first turn of player $1$. If they land a heads on their first flip, they are guaranteed the win. Otherwise, if they land a tails, a lot must happen for them to get another shot. Thus, we should use Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens at the first flip. Let $\alpha$ be the probability that player $1$ wins when they are first to flip.

$$$$

With probability $p$, person $1$ gets a heads on their first turn and automatically wins. Otherwise, with probability $1-p$, they land a tails on their first turn. For player $1$ to get another shot at winning, the other $n-1$ people must all land tails, which occurs with probability $(1-p)^{n-1}$. If any person lands a heads, that person wins, meaning player $1$ would not win. If all players land a tails, then the coin goes back to player $1$, and they have probability $\alpha$ of winning in this case, as the situation of the game is completely unchanged from the fact that the coin went through a full revolution and is back at player $1$. Therefore, by Law of Total Probability, $$\alpha = p + (1-p)(1-p)^{n-1}\alpha \iff \alpha = \dfrac{p}{1-(1-p)^n}$$ With the given values, the answer is $\dfrac{81}{211}$.
hints: Use Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens for the first flip of player $1$. If they land a tails, what must occur to get another shot?

title: Big 6
statement: $5$ standard fair $6-$sided dice are rolled. We sum the $3$ largest upfaces showing. Find the probability that the sum is $18$.
solution: For the sum to be $18$, there must be at least $3$ $6$s showing among the dice, as we only sum the three largest values. Therefore, the event that the sum is $18$ just the equivalent to the event $\{N \geq 3\}$, where $N$ is the number $6$s that appear. As $N$ is counting the number of $6$s that appear in the $5$ rolls, and each roll is independent, we can conclude that $N \sim \text{Bin}(5, 1/6)$, as there are $5$ trials and a probability $1/6$ per trial of obtaining a $6$. Thus, we have $$P(N \geq 3) = P(N = 3) + P(N = 4) + P(N = 5) = \binom{5}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^3\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2 + \binom{5}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^4\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right) + \binom{5}{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^5 = \dfrac{23}{648}$$
hints: For the sum to be $18$, there must be at least $3$ $6$s showing among the dice.

title: Sumdard Deviation
statement: You have $k$ identical sets of $n$ cards with the values $1-n$ on the cards. You pick one card from each set and add all of them up. Find the standard deviation of the sum when $k = 4$ and $n = 7$.
solution:
The first important fact is that the $k$ decks are all independent, as they are all separated. We are looking to find the standard deviation of the sum of values, which is related to the variance. Thus, the variance of a sum formula would be helpful. Let $V_i$ be the value of the card selected from deck $i$, $1 \leq i \leq k$. $T = V_1 + \dots + V_k$ gives the total sum of all $k$ cards. We want $\sigma_T = \sqrt{\text{Var}(T)}$. To compute $\text{Var}(T)$, we can note that since $V_1,\dots, V_k$ are independent (from the fact that the decks are independent) and identically distributed (since the decks are identical), $\text{Var}(T) = k\text{Var}(V_1)$. $\text{Var}(V_1)$ is the variance of a value selected uniformly at random from one of the decks. This could be modelled as $V_1 \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, as the card is selected uniformly at random from the deck. To compute variance, we must compute $\text{Var}(V_1) = E[V_1^2] - (E[V_1])^2$, as this is the base formula when we don't have a quick way of computing it.

$$$$

We know that $$E[V_1] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n iP(V_1 = i) = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n i = \dfrac{n+1}{2}$$ Note that $P(V_1 = i) = \dfrac{1}{n}$ by the fact that $V_1$ is discrete uniform. Similarly, we have $$E[V_1^2] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n i^2P(V_1 = i) = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = \dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = \dfrac{2n^2 + 3n + 1}{6}$$

Thus, we have $\text{Var}(V_1) = \dfrac{2n^2 + 3n + 1}{6} - \dfrac{(n+1)^2}{4} = \dfrac{n^2 - 1}{12}$. Therefore, $\text{Var}(T) = k\cdot \dfrac{n^2 - 1}{12}$, so $\sigma_T = \sqrt{\dfrac{k(n^2-1)}{12}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $4$.
hints: The $k$ decks are all independent. Let $V_i$ be the value of the card selected from deck $i$, $1 \leq i \leq k$. Then $T = V_1 + \dots + V_k$ gives the total sum of all $k$ cards.

title: Conditional RNG I
statement: Adam selects a uniformly random number in the interval $(0,1)$. If Adam selects the value $x$, Eve selects a uniformly random number in $(x,1)$. Let $V$ be the value that Eve selects. Find $E[V]$.
solution: The first item to do is to set up Adam and Eve's choices as distributions. Namely, $A \sim U(0, 1)$, as Adam selects a uniform real number on $(0,1)$. Then, given $A = a$ i.e. Adam picks $a$, Eve picks a uniform real number on $(a,1)$, so $V \mid A = a \sim U(a, 1)$. Since we know the distribution of Eve's choice given Adam's choice, we should use Law of Total Expectation. Namely, we have $E[V] = E[E[V \mid A]]$. As $V \mid A \sim U(A, 1)$, $E[V \mid A] = \dfrac{1+A}{2}$, so $$E[V] = E[\dfrac{1+A]{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}(1 + E[A]) = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
hints: Set up Adam and Eve's choices as distributions. Since you know the distribution of Eve's choice given Adam's choice, you should use Law of Total Expectation.

title: One Correlation I
statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are random variables such that $\text{Corr}(X, Y) = 1$ and $\sigma_Y < \sigma_X$. Find $\text{Corr}(X+Y, X-Y)$.
solution:
Since we are looking to compute a correlation, we should write out explicitly what we want to compute. Namely, $\text{Corr}(X+Y, X-Y) = \dfrac{\text{Cov}(X+Y, X-Y)}{\sigma_{X+Y}\sigma_{X-Y}}$. Let's start by computing the two standard deviations.

$$$$

We have that $\sigma_{X+Y} = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X+Y)}$, and we can use the variance of a sum formula to find $\text{Var}(X+Y)$. This becomes $$\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 + 2 \cdot (1 \cdot \sigma_X\sigma_Y) = (\sigma_X + \sigma_Y)^2$$ The second equality is by substituting in $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \text{Corr}(X, Y) \sigma_X\sigma_Y$. Similarly, we have $$\text{Var}(X-Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) - 2\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 - 2\text{Cov}(X, Y) = (\sigma_X - \sigma_Y)^2$$ For the covariance, we can use the use bilinearity of covariance to obtain $$\text{Cov}(X+Y, X-Y) = \text{Cov}(X, X) + \text{Cov}(X, -Y) + \text{Cov}(Y, X) + \text{Cov}(Y, -Y) = \text{Var}(X) - \text{Var}(Y) = \sigma_X^2 - \sigma_Y^2$$ The middle two terms cancel. By bilinearity, $\text{Cov}(X, -Y) = -\text{Cov}(X, Y)$. By symmetry, $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \text{Cov}(Y, X)$, so the two terms cancel out. Plugging into the definition of correlation, $$\text{Corr}(X+Y, X-Y) = \dfrac{\sigma_X^2 - \sigma_Y^2}{\sqrt{(\sigma_X + \sigma_Y)^2(\sigma_X - \sigma_Y)^2}} = \dfrac{(\sigma_X + \sigma_Y)(\sigma_X - \sigma_Y)}{(\sigma_X + \sigma_Y)|\sigma_X - \sigma_Y|} = \text{sign}(\sigma_X - \sigma_Y)$$ In the above, we need absolute values around $\sigma_X - \sigma_Y$ because of the fact that, for general real $x$, $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$, as $(-x)^2 = x^2$ and the square root only outputs positive values. $\text{sign}(x)$ evaluates to $1$ if $x$ is positive and $-1$ if $x$ is negative. In this case, as $\sigma_X > \sigma_Y$, $\sigma_X - \sigma_Y > 0$, so this implies $\text{Corr}(X+Y, X-Y) = 1$.
hints: Use the definition of correlation coefficient to see that you need to compute $\cov{X+Y}{X-Y}, \sigma_{X+Y},$ and $\sigma_{X-Y}$. Use properties of variance and covariance to obtain these. Be careful of signs.

title: Valid Upper Bound
statement: Suppose that $(X,Y) \sim \text{BVN}(0,0,\sigma^2,\sigma^2,\rho)$. From Chebyshev's Inequality, find an upper bound on $\mathbb{P}[|X-Y| \geq \sigma]$ when $\sigma^2 = 4$ and $\rho = 3/4$.
solution: Since $X$ and $Y$ are marginally $N(0,\sigma^2)$, they both have mean $0$. As the random variable needs to be centered to apply Chebyshev's Inequality, we must ensure that $X-Y$ is centered inside the absolute values. However, this is the case, as $E[X-Y] = E[X] - E[Y] = 0$, so we can now directly apply Chebyshev's Inequality to compute $$P(|X-Y| \geq \sigma) \leq \dfrac{\text{Var}(X-Y)}{\sigma^2}$$ To compute $\text{Var}(X-Y),$ we can use the variance of a sum formula to obtain $$\text{Var}(X-Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) - 2\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 - 2\rho\sigma^2 = 2\sigma^2(1-\rho)$$ Therefore, $$P(|X-Y| \geq \sigma) \leq \dfrac{2\sigma^2(1-\rho)}{\sigma^2} = 2(1-\rho)$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.
hints: Since $X$ and $Y$ are marginally $N(0,\sigma^2)$, they both have mean $0$. What can you say about $X-Y$ then?

title: Product Limit
statement: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be IID random variables with finite mean $\mu_X$ and variance $\sigma_X^2$ and $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be another sequence of IID random variables with finite mean $\mu_Y$ and variance $\sigma_Y^2$. Note that the $X_i$ and $Y_i$ sequences are independent of each other. Consider the sequence $Z_i = X_iY_i$. Does the sequence $$\dfrac{Z_1 + Z_2 + \dots + Z_n}{n}$$ converge to some distribution as $n \rightarrow \infty$? If it does, state the sum of the mean and variance of the distribution. If it doesn't, answer $-100$. Answer this when $\mu_X = 5, \mu_Y = 6, \sigma_X^2 = 25,$ and $\sigma_Y^2 = 36$.
solution: The $Z_i$ random variables are IID and have finite mean. Therefore, the Law of Large Numbers applies here. Note that this is not the Central Limit Theorem because the random variables are not being standardized. Namely, we have that $$\dfrac{Z_1 + \dots + Z_n}{n} \rightarrow E[Z_1] = E[X_1Y_1] = E[X_1]E[Y_1] = \mu_X\mu_Y$$ The expectation of the product separates out due to the independence of the $X_i$ and $Y_i$ sequences. With the specified values, the answer is $30$.
hints: The $Z_i$ random variables are IID and have finite mean. The Law of Large Numbers applies here.

title: Equal Unequal Dice
statement: You roll $k$ fair dice labelled $1-k$. The $i$th die has $n_i \geq 1$ sides and has the values $1-n_i$ on the sides. If all the dice are rolled, find the probability that they all show the same value. Solve this when $n = 4$ and $n_i = 8 - 2|i - 2.5|$.
solution: For all the dice to show the same value, a common value that all of the dice show must be selected. Since the $i$th die has the values $1-n_i$ on the sides, the maximum value that all the dice can show is $\min(n_1,\dots, n_k)$, as all the dice need to be able to show the value, and the maximum value that all the dice share in common is $\min(n_1,\dots, n_k)$. Therefore, there are $\min(n_1,\dots, n_k)$ outcomes where the dice all show the same value, which correspond to all the dice showing $1,2,\dots, \min(n_1,\dots, n_k)$. The total number of outcomes that can be obtained from the dice is $n_1\dots n_k$, as there are $n_i$ outcomes for die $i$, so we can use the multiplication rule to get the total number of outcomes. Thus, the probability that all $k$ dice show the same value is $$\dfrac{\min(n_1,\dots, n_k)}{n_1\dots n_k}$$ With the specified values here, the answer is $\dfrac{5}{5^2 \cdot 7^2} = \dfrac{1}{245}$.
hints: How many ways can the value that they all match on be selected? How many total outcomes are there?

title: Bad Dealer
statement: Scott is a poker player. He sucks at dealing, so as he starts dealing a standard deck, he immediately drops 2 random cards. He decides to give up and flip over the first card at the top of the deck from the remaining $50-$card deck. What is the probability it is a club?
solution: Removing $2$ cards from the deck and then asking that the next one is a club is essentially the same as the asking if the $3$rd card drawn at random from a standard deck is a club when dealing without replacement. By the exchangeability of sampling without replacement, this is the same as asking the probability that the first card drawn is a club, which is $13/52 = 1/4$.
hints: Removing $2$ cards from the deck and then asking that the next one is a club is essentially the same as the asking if the $3$rd card drawn at random from a standard deck is a club when dealing without replacement.

title: Fair and Unfair Die
statement: Abby has two dice with the values $1-6$ on the sides. One die is fair, while the other is weighted with probabilities $p_i$ for side $i$, $1 \leq i \leq 6$. Abby rolls both dice. Find the probability that the sum of their upfaces is even when $p_i = \dfrac{i}{21}$.
solution: To obtain an even sum, it must be the case that either both dice are even or both are odd. We can compute the probability of each of these two cases. Let $p$ be the probability of rolling an even value on the weighted die. Then $1-p$ is the probability of an odd value appearing on the weighted die. On the fair die, there is probability $1/2$ of showing an even value and probability $1/2$ showing an odd value. Therefore, the probability both are even is $\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot p$, as the dice are independent of one another. Similarly, the probability both are odd is $\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1-p)$. Therefore, as these two cases are disjoint, we can add their probabilities together to obtain the probability of an even sum. This yields a probability of $$\dfrac{1}{2} \left(p + (1-p)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$ This result holds irrespective of the weighing of the second die, so the answer is $1/2$.
hints: Let $p$ be the probability of rolling an even value on the weighted die. Then $1-p$ is the probability of an odd value appearing on the weighted die. Condition on if an even or odd value appears on the weighted die.

title: Floor Equality
statement: Suppose $X,Y \sim U(0, n)$ for some integer $n > 0$. Find the probability that $\lfloor X+Y \rfloor = \lfloor X \rfloor + \lfloor Y \rfloor$ when $n = 100$.
solution:
One can write any real number $x$ as $x = \lfloor x \rfloor + \{x\}$, where $\{x\}$ is the fractional part of $x$ (for example, $3.41 = 3 + 0.41$, and $0.41$ is the fractional part). Therefore, $x+y = \lfloor x+y \rfloor + \{x+y\}$, and similar for $x$ and $y$ individually. Thus, the condition we need to have true is $\{x+y\} = \{x\} + \{y\}$. This holds true exactly when $\{x\} + \{y\} < 1$, as if it is at least $1$, $\{x+y\} = \{x\} + \{y\} - 1$, as there would be able to be another integer subtracted out of $x+y$. 
$$$$

Using this work above, we must compute $P(\{X\) + \{Y\} < 1}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform on $(0,n)$ and $n$ is an integer, the fractional components of $X$ and $Y$ are uniform on $(0,1)$. This should make intuitive sense, since if $X$ is uniform on an integer-length interval, the fractional components should also be uniform, as all that is done in the fractional component is integer subtraction to make $X$ wrap around $(0,1)$ many times. This can be formally proven as follows: $P(\{X\) \leq x} = P(\displaystyle \bigcup_{k=0)^{n-1}\{k \leq X \leq k+x\}}$, as the fractional component being at most $x$ means that $X$ is within $x$ of the previous integer $k$ for some $k$. This generates $n$ intervals of length $x$ within the support $(0,n)$. These are also disjoint, as we must have $x < 1$ and the spacing between intervals is $1$. Therefore, as $X$ is uniform, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities of events. The total length of the event of interest is $nx$, as there are $n$ disjoint intervals of length $x$ by the above. The total support is of length $n$, so $P(\{X\) \leq x} = x$, which is the CDF of a $U(0, 1)$ distribution.

$$$$

Now that this is proven, we know that $\{X\}, \{Y\} \sim U(0, 1)$ IID. This allows us to compute $P(\{X\) + \{Y\} < 1}$ quite easily. Namely, we can draw out the region in the plane and note that this is the region below the line $y = 1-x$ inside the unit square $(0,1) \times (0,1)$. This region is exactly $1/2$ of the area of the support, so as we are dealing with uniform random variables, we can conclude that the probability is $1/2$, independent of $n$.
hints: One can write any real number $x$ as $x = \floor{x} + \{x\}$, where $\{x\}$ is the fractional part of $x$ (for example, $3.41 = 3 + 0.41$, and $0.41$ is the fractional part). Therefore, the condition is here is that $\{x+y\} = \{x\} + \{y\}$. When does this hold true?

title: Tricky Die
statement: You have a $6-$sided die before you with the values $1-6$ on the sides. The $6$ sides $1-6$, respectively, have probabilities $1/6, 1/6, 1/4 - x, 1/4 - 2x, 1/6,$ and $3x$ of appearing. Find the value of $x$ that minimizes the probability of obtaining a sum of $7$ when rolling the die twice.
solution:
You can obtain a sum of $7$ by obtaining $(1,6), (2,5),$ or $(3,4)$ in some order on the dice. There are $2! = 2$ arrangements of the values onto these dice per pair. To get the total probability of obtaining a sum of $7$, we should add up the probabilities of obtaining some permutation of each of these pairs as a function of $x$.

$$$$

$1$ and $6$ have probability $1/6$ and $3x$ of appearing, respectively. So, the probability here is $2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot 3x = x$ of obtaining some permutation of $(1,6)$. 

$$$$

$2$ and $5$ both have probability $1/6$ of appearing, so some permutation of this appears with probability $2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{18}$. 

$$$$

Lastly, $3$ and $4$ appear with respective probabilities $1/4 - x$ and $1/4 - 2x$, so the probability of some permutation of these appearing is $2 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}-x\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{4} -2x\right) = 4x^2 - \dfrac{3}{2}x + \dfrac{1}{8}$.

$$$$

 Adding all of these disjoint cases up, the probability, as a function of $x$, of obtaining a sum of $7$ is, $$p(x) = 4x^2 - \dfrac{3}{2}x + \dfrac{1}{8} + x + \dfrac{1}{16} = 4x^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{3}{16}$$ 

We need to optimize this in $x$. This can be done by taking the derivative. Namely, $p'(x) = 8x - 1/2 = 0 \iff x = \dfrac{1}{16}$.
hints: You can obtain a sum of $7$ by obtaining $(1,6), (2,5),$ or $(3,4)$ in some order on the dice. Add up the probabilities of obtaining some permutation of each of these pairs as a function of $x$.

title: Conditional Bivariate
statement: Suppose that $M,S \sim \exponential{1}$ IID. Given that $M = \mu$ and $S = \sigma$, $(X,Y) \sim \text{BVN}(\mu,\mu,\sigma^2,\sigma^2,\rho)$, where $|\rho| \leq 1$ is fixed. Compute $\text{Var}(Y)$.
solution:
The transformation of standard normals that leads to the bivariate normals in question, given $\mu$ and $\sigma$ is $X = \mu + \sigma Z_1$ and $Y = \mu + \sigma(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2)$. However, $\sigma$ and $\mu$ are now random variables themselves. Therefore, we know that $Y = M + S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2)$, where $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are IID $N(0,1)$. 

$$$$

We have then that $$\text{Var}(Y) = \text{Var}(M + S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2) = \text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2))$$ This is because the two terms are independent. The first term is simple: $\text{Var}(M) = 1$ by known formulas of the exponential distribution. 

$$$$

To compute the second term, we know how to compute this given the value of $S$, so we should use Law of Total Variance, conditioning on the value of $S$. Doing this, $$\text{Var}(S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2)) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2) \mid S)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2) \mid S])$$ The second term is just $0$ because $$\mathbb{E}[S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2) \mid S] = S\mathbb{E}[\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2] = S\rhoE[Z_1] + S\sqrt{1-\rho^2}E[Z_2] = 0$$ The first term is $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$, as $$\text{Var}(S(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2) \mid S) = S^2(\text{Var}(\rho Z_1) + \text{Var}(\sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2)) = S^2\rho^2 \text{Var}(Z_1) + S^2(1-\rho^2)\text{Var}(Z_2) = S^2$$ Thus, $\mathbb{E}[S^2] = 2$ by known formulas for the exponential distribution, so our answer is $\text{Var}(Y) = 3$.
hints: Use the definition of the transformation that leads to the bivariate normal $X = \mu + \sigma Z_1$ and $Y = \mu + \sigma(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z_2)$. However, $\sigma$ and $\mu$ are now random variables themselves.
The Law of Total Expectation and Law of Total Variance will help

title: Sniper
statement: A sniper is shooting at targets. There are $r$ columns of identical targets, with column $i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, having $n_i$ targets in it stacked vertically. The sniper first selects a column and then shoots the lowest-hanging target in that column that is not broken. Once a column is out of targets, it is no longer able to be selected. In how many distinct orders can the sniper break all the targets? Solve this when $n = 5$ and $n_i = i$.
solution:
Each order of breaking the targets is equivalent to some anagram of length $n_1 + \dots + n_r$, where the $i$th spot being $1 \leq j \leq n$ is saying that a target in column $j$ was shot on the $i$th turn. In other words, we can view the sequence of breaking as a string of length $n_1 + \dots + n_r$, where there are $n_i$ occurrences of $i$ in the string. This is because every target needs to be broken, and there are $n_i$ targets in column $i$, so the sniper must shoot at column $i$ $n_i$ times to make it completely empty.

$$$$

The question of counting anagrams is a much simpler one. The number of anagrams is given by $\binom{n_1 + \dots + n_r}{n_1,\dots, n_r} = \dfrac{(n_1 + \dots + n_r)!}{n_1!\dots n_r!}$. With the specific values in the question, the answer is $\dfrac{15!}{1!2!3!4!5!} = 37837800$.
hints: Each order of breaking the targets is equivalent to some anagram of length $n_1 + \dots + n_r$, where the $i$th spot being $1 \leq j \leq n$ is saying that a target in column $j$ was shot on the $i$th turn.

title: Uniform Variance
statement: Suppose that $X \sim U(a, b)$. Find $\text{Var}(X)$ when $a = 0$ and $b = 1$.
solution:
The best approach here is to write $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. Both of these can be computed via LOTUS easily. The PDF of $X \sim U(a, b)$ is $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{b-a}I_{(a,b)}(x)$. Therefore, we have $$E[X] = \int_a^b xf(x)dx = \int_0^1 x \cdot \dfrac{1}{b-a}dx = \dfrac{1}{2(b-a)}x^2\big|_a^b = \dfrac{b^2-a^2}{2(b-a)} = \dfrac{b+a}{2}$$

Similarly, we can compute $$E[X^2] = \int_a^b x^2f(x)dx = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{b-a}dx = \dfrac{b^3-a^3}{3(b-a)} = \dfrac{a^2 + ab + b^2}{3}$$ Plugging these values in and performing some algebraic reduction, we have $$\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 + ab}{3} - \dfrac{a^2 + 2ab + b^2}{4} = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}$$ With the requested values, the answer is $1/12$.
hints: The best approach is to write $\var{X} = \ev{X^2} - (\ev{X})^2$. Both of these can be computed via LOTUS.

title: Cookie Cruncher
statement: Dan enjoys savoring his food, so takes a uniformly random time between $2$ and $7$ minutes to eat a cookie. If he has not finished eating the cookie after $4$ minutes, find the probability that Dan finishes eating the cookie in the next minute.
solution: Let $T$ be the amount of time that Dan takes to eat the cookie. We are looking to compute $P(T \leq 4 + 1 \mid T \geq 4)$, as we want the probability that he finishes the cookie in the next minute given he took at least $4$ minutes. Using the definition of conditional probability, $$P(T \leq 5 \mid T \geq 4) = \dfrac{P(4 \leq T \leq 5)}{P(T \geq 4)}$$ Since $T \sim U(2, 7)$ by the question, we can take ratios of lengths of intervals to compute the probability. In particular, $P(T \geq 4) = 3/5$, as the total interval is of length $7-2 = 5$, while the event is of length $7-4=3$. Similarly, we have $P(4 \leq T \leq 5) = 1/5$, as the event is of length $1$ here. Therefore, the answer is $1/3$.
hints: Let $T$ be the amount of time that Dan takes to eat the cookie. We are looking to compute $\prob{T \leq 4 + 1 \mid T \geq 4}$, as we want the probability that he finishes the cookie in the next minute given he took at least $4$ minutes.

title: Non-Decreasing Numbers
statement: Fix $n \geq 1$. A sequence of digits $x_1x_2\dots x_n$ is said to be $\textit{non-decreasing}$ if $x_i \leq x_{i+1}$ for $1 \leq i \leq n-1$ and each $0 \leq x_i \leq 9$. How many non-decreasing $n$ digit strings exist when $n = 8$? There are no restrictions on how many times a digit can be used, and strings are allowed to start with $0$. Some examples with $n = 8$ are $00112234, 11111111,$ and $15678999$.
solution: The total number of digits in the string is $n$. We know that the string is non-decreasing left to right. Each string has a certain number of $0,1,\dots,9$ inside. For example, $00112234$ could be written as a tuple $(2,2,2,1,1,0,0,0,0,0)$, where the $i$th element of the list represents the number of times $i-1$ (since it is really $0-$indexed) appears in the passcode. More generally, if $n_i$, $0 \leq i \leq 9$, represents the number of times that $i$ appears in the passcode, then $n_0 + n_1 + \dots + n_9 = n$, as the number of times that all the digits appear in total must be $n$. The only restriction is that $n_i \geq 0$ is an integer, as there must be a non-negative integer amount of occurrences of each digit in the string. We can create a one-to-one correspondence between solutions of the above equation and non-decreasing strings. Namely, the solution $(n_0,n_1,\dots,n_9)$ creates the string that starts with $n_0$ $0$s, then has $n_1$ $1$s concatenated to the right of it, and so on. This guarantees that the string is non-decreasing, as we concatenate the characters in value order. Therefore, counting the number of non-decreasing strings is equivalent to counting the number of non-negative solutions of the above equation. By stars and bars, this is $\binom{n+10-1}{10-1} = \binom{n+9}{9}$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $\binom{17}{9} = 24310$.
hints: The total number of digits in the string is $n$. We know that the string is non-decreasing left to right. Each string has a certain number of $0,1,\dots,9$ inside. Can you relate this to some equation?

title: Colorful Run I
statement: A bowl consists of $n$ red and $n$ blue marbles. Marbles are drawn from this bag one-by-one without replacement until there are no marbles left in the bag. The order that the marbles are drawn in is noted. Once the marbles are drawn out, you count the number of runs in your sequence, where a run is defined as a maximal contiguous sequence of the same outcome. For example, $BBRBRR$ has $4$ runs. Find the expected amount of runs in your sequence when $n = 100$.
solution: The number of runs is equal to the number of starts of runs, as every single run must have a start. Since we are looking for the expected count of something occurring in sampling without replacement, linearity of expectation is the way to go. The first task is to set up appropriate indicators. Since we want to count the expected number of runs, let $X_i$ be the indicator of the event that the $i$th marble drawn out is the start of a new run. $T = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{2n}$ gives the total number of runs in our sequence. Note that all of these except one are identically distributed. Namely, $X_1 = 1$ always, as there is no marble prior to it that it needs to differ in color from, so it must be the start of a run. However, the other $2n-1$ random variables are all exchangeable, as we are sampling without replacement and the probability of being the start of a new run only depends on there being a previous marble to compare to, in which all of them have a marble to compare to. By linearity of expectation and exchangeability, $$E[T] = 1 + (2n-1)E[X_2]$$ Note that we have to choose $X_2$ since $X_1$ has a different distribution than the rest. $E[X_2]$ is the probability that the second marble drawn is the start of a new run. This means that the color of the first and second marbles drawn differ. Since each marble color is equally likely for the first draw, we can fix it arbitrarily. WLOG, say it is red. To start a new run, the second marble must be blue. There are $n$ blue marbles in the bowl at this point out of $2n-1$ total, as we sample without replacement, so $E[X_2] = \dfrac{n}{2n-1}$. Plugging this in, $E[T] = n+1$. With $n = 100$, the answer is $101$.
hints: The number of runs is equal to the number of starts of runs, as every single run must have a start.
Let $X_i$ be the indicator of the event that the $i$th marble drawn out is the start of a new run. $T = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{2n}$ gives the total number of runs.
All of these except one are identically distributed.

title: Multiplicative Exponential
statement: Suppose that $X,Y \sim \exponential{\lambda}$ IID and fix $k > 0$. Find $P(Y > kX)$ when $\lambda = 3$ and $k = 5$.
solution:
Since we are looking to compute some type of probability in two random variables and the region isn't symmetric, we should sketch the region out in the plane and integrate over the joint PDF of $X$ and $Y$.

$$$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the joint PDF of $X$ and $Y$ is $f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}I_{(0,\infty)}(x) \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda y}\I{0}{\infty}(y)$. We can now set up the integral as $$P(Y > kX) = \int_0^{\infty} \int_{kx}^{\infty} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda y}dydx = \int_0^{\infty} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\int_{kx}^{\infty} \lambda e^{-\lambda y}dy = \int_0^{\infty} \lambda e^{-\lambda(k+1)x}dx = \dfrac{1}{k+1}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/6$. 

$$$$

Note that there is an intuitive interpretation of this. We can view the exponential random variables as waiting times until some event occurs. $kX$ is essentially scaling time by $k$ so that the waiting time between events is $k$ times as long. Therefore, the expected number of events that occur per unit time is now $\lambda/k$ instead of $\lambda$. Thus, the event $\{Y > kX\}$ is really saying that one of the events that occurs with average rate $\lambda/k$ per unit time is the first to occur. The total average rate of events per unit time is $\lambda + \lambda/k$, and $\lambda/k$ of those belong to the process for which $X$ is an interarrival distribution, so the probability that the first event to occur is from the process with $X$ is $$\dfrac{\lambda/k}{\lambda +\lambda/k} = \dfrac{1}{1+k}$$
hints: Sketch this region out in the plane and integrate over the joint PDF of $X$ and $Y$.

title: Less Than Exponential
statement: Suppose $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_1)$ and $Y \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_2)$ are independent. Find $\mathbb{P}[X < Y]$ when $\lambda_1 = 4$ and $\lambda_2 = 6$
solution:
Note that $X$ and $Y$ are not necessarily IID, so we can't just say it is $1/2$. However, we can use the case where $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$ as a litmus test for the solution to ensure that it is $1/2$ in that case. Computing this probability is best done by integrating over the joint PDF, as the random variables are not identically distributed. We want to integrate over $0 < x < y < \infty$, as that is the region where $x < y$. The joint PDF is easily obtained by multiplying the PDFs of $X$ and $Y$ together to get $f(x,y) = \lambda_1\lambda_2e^{-(\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 y)}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)I_{(0,\infty)}(y)$. The integral we must evaluate is $$P(X < Y) = \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \int_{x}^{\infty} \lambda_1\lambda_2e^{-(\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 y)}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)I_{(0,\infty)}(y) dydx = \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \lambda_1 e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)x}dx = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2} \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)x}dx$$ The interior of the last integral is the PDF of an $\text{Exp}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$ distribution. We are integrating this PDF over its entire support, so the integral must be $1$. Therefore, the probability in question is $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$. 

$$$$

Intuitively, this answer makes sense. Suppose you have a machine producing red cards at a rate of $\lambda_1$ per time unit on average and $\lambda_2$ blue cards per time unit on average, independently of one another. Then the probability that the first card produced is red should intuitively just be the average amount of red cards produced in the period, $\lambda_1$, out of the average total amount of cards produced in the period, $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$. When $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, we can see that the fraction above reduces to $1/2$, which is what we would expect in the IID case. With the specified values in the problem, the answer is $2/5$.
hints: Note that $X$ and $Y$ are not necessarily IID, so we can't just say it is $1/2$.
Computing this probability is best done by integrating over the joint PDF, as the random variables are not identically distributed.

title: Sum Diff Normal
statement: Let $X \sim N(1,4)$, $Y \sim N(3,2)$, and $Z \sim N(2,6)$ be independent. Find $\mathbb{P}[X + Y - 2Z \geq 0]$.
solution: Sums and differences of independent normal distributions are normally distributed. In particular, if $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are all independent normal distributions with $X_i \sim N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)$, then $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim N\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \mu_i,\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2\right)$. We also know that scaling normals by a constant also results in a normal distribution. In particular, if $X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $aX + b \sim N(a\mu + b,a^2\sigma^2)$. Apply these values, we have that the mean of $X + Y - 2Z$ is $1 + 3 - 2(2) = 0$. Similarly, the variance is $4 + 2 + 2^2 \cdot 6 = 30$. In other words, let $W \sim N(0,30)$. We really want to compute $P(W \geq 0)$. However, note that the normal random variable PDF is symmetric about its mean, which is $0$ in this case. Therefore, the probability that it is greater than or less than its mean are equal, and hence must both be $1/2$.
hints: Sums and differences of independent normal distributions are also normal. What are the parameters?

title: Die Diff
statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ the random value that appear when two standard fair $n-$sided dice with the values $1-n$ on the sides are rolled. Compute $E[|X-Y|]$ when $n = 10$.
solution:
To get some intuition, draw out a grid for the standard $n = 6$ case. The region where $|X-Y| = 1$ is one off the diagonal, which has $5$ outcomes on each side (above and below). Similarly, $|X-Y| = 2$ is two off the diagonal, which has $4$ outcomes on each side. Note that $5 = 6-1$ and $4 = 6-2$. More generally, with $n$ sides and $1 \leq k \leq n-1$, the event $|X-Y| = k$ is $k$ off the diagonal and consists of $n-k$ values above and below. Therefore, of the $n^2$ total outcomes, exactly $2(n-k)$ of them satisfy $|X-Y| = k$. Since the dice are fair, we can conclude that for $1 \leq k \leq n-1$, $P(|X-Y| = k) = \dfrac{2(n-k)}{n^2}$. Note that while $|X-Y| = 0$ has positive probability, it does not change our expected value, as the term in the expected value expression will be $0 \cdot P(|X-Y| = 0) = 0$.

$$$$

We can use this with the definition of expected value to compute $E[|X-Y|]$. Namely, $$E[|X-Y|] = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k P(|X-Y| = k) = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k \cdot \dfrac{2(n-k)}{n^2} = \dfrac{2}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k - \dfrac{2}{n^2}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k^2 = \dfrac{2}{n} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} - \dfrac{2}{n^2} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6} = \dfrac{n^2-1}{3n}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $\dfrac{99}{30} = 3.3$.
hints: Draw out a grid for the standard $n = 6$ case and note the regions where $|X-Y|$ takes the values $0,1,2,3,4,$ and $5$. See if you can generate this to $n$.

title: Larger Value
statement: A box has $n$ chips labeled with distinct numbers $1$ to $n$. We draw two chips at random without replacement and record their values. Find the probability that the larger of the two values is $1$ larger than the smaller of the two values when $n = 20$.
solution: Let $(a,b)$ represent the outcome that the first value is $a$ and the second value is $b \neq a$. We want to find the probability that the outcome is $(i,i+1)$ or $(i+1,i)$ for some integer $i$. These outcomes are the ones where the smaller value (which is $i$) is one smaller than the larger value (which is $i+1$). We have have $1 \leq i \leq n-1$, as the largest possible pair would be $(n-1,n)$ or $(n,n-1)$. To account for both possible cases, there are $2(n-1)$ such pairs. Since we do consider ordering distinct when counting the favorable outcomes above, we should do so in the denominator too. There are $n$ ways to pick the value for the first draw, and then $n-1$ ways to pick it for the second draw, as we remove the outcome from the first draw. Therefore, the probability of this event is $$\dfrac{2(n-1)}{n(n-1)} = \dfrac{2}{n}$$ With $n = 20$, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{10}$.
hints: Let $(a,b)$ represent the outcome that the first value is $a$ and the second value is $b \neq a$. We want to find the probability that the outcome is $(i,i+1)$ or $(i+1,i)$ for some integer $i$. How many such pairs are in this form? How many total pairs are there?

title: Sammythewhale I
statement: Consider the phrase "SAMMYTHEWHALE". Ben at random rearranges the letters in the phrase. Find the probability that Ben recreates the original phrase after rearrangement.
solution: Ben is manking an anagram of "SAMMYTHEWHALE" when he shuffles the letters around. Therefore, we need to count the number of (distinct) anagrams of "SAMMYTHEWHALE". There are 2 E's, 2 M's, 2 A's, and 2 H's. All other letters only have 1 occurrence in the string. Thus, there are $\binom{13}{2,2,2,2}$ distinct anagrams of the phrase. Only one of them is SAMMYTHEWHALE, so as each anagram is equally likely, the probability is $$\dfrac{1}{\displaystyle \binom{13}{2,2,2,2}} = \dfrac{1}{389188800}$$
hints: Ben is making an anagram of "SAMMYTHEWHALE" when he shuffles the letters around. How many distinct anagrams are there? How many of those are the original string?

title: Hat Matcher I
statement: $n$ men attend a party. Since it is formal, there is a hat closet at the entrance. All $n$ men put their distinct hats into the closet at the beginning of the party. At the end, the power at the party goes out! Each man goes into the closet and selects a hat uniformly at random. Let $p(n)$ be the the probability that none of the $n$ men receives their hat back. Find $p(5)$.
solution: Let $H_i$ be the event that person $i$ receives their hat back. We want to compute $\displaystyle P(\bigcap_{i=1)^n H_i^c}$, the probability of the event that nobody receives their hat back. The $H_i$ events are clearly not independent, as the knowledge that one person does not receive their hat back automatically implies that someone else can't receive their hat back, as the other person took a hat belonging to a different person. These events are also not disjoint, as it is possible that multiple people do not get their hat back. Therefore, the best approach is to work with the complement, which is to compute the probability at least one person receives their hat back. In mathematical terms, $\displaystyle P(\bigcap_{i=1)^n H_i^c} = 1 - P(\bigcup_{i=1)^n H_i}$. Our goal is to now compute $\displaystyle P(\bigcup_{i=1)^n H_i}$.  Since these events are not disjoint, we will need to use the inclusion-exclusion formula. As the labels on the people are arbitrary, the events are exchangeable, so all intersection probabilities are the same. Namely, we have that $$P(\bigcup_{i=1)^n H_i} = \binom{n}{1}P(H_1) - \binom{n}{2}P(H_1\cap H_2) + \dots + (-1)^{n+1}\binom{n}{n}P(\bigcap_{i=1)^n H_i} = \sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{i+1}\binom{n}{i}P(\bigcap_{k=1)^i H_k}$$ Our remaining task is to compute $\displaystyle P(\bigcap_{k=1)^i H_k}$. This is the event that all of the first $k$ people obtain their hats back. When drawing out the hats from the closet, we are essentially permuting the hats to the people. Thus, there are $n!$ total permutations of the hats to the people. To compute the number of arrangements where the first $i$ people have their hat returned to them, we note that each of the first $i$ people have their outcome fixed already: they receive back the hat they started with. Therefore, all that is left is permuting the remaining $n-i$ hats to the other $n-i$ people that are yet to draw, as the first $i$ are fixed. There are $(n-i)!$ total ways to do this, so $\displaystyle P(\bigcap_{k=1)^i H_k} = \dfrac{(n-i)!}{n!}$. Plugging this in, $$P(\bigcup_{i=1)^n H_i} = \sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{i+1}\binom{n}{i} \cdot \dfrac{(n-i)!}{n!} = \sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{i+1} \cdot \dfrac{n!}{i!(n-i)!} \cdot \dfrac{(n-i)!}{n!} = \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{(-1)^{i+1}}{i!}$$ This sum can't be reduced any further, so substituting back into our original statement, $$p(n) = P(\bigcap_{i=1)^n H_i^c} = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{(-1)^{i+1}}{i!} = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-1)^i}{i!} = \sum_{i=0}^n \dfrac{(-1)^i}{i!}$$ We were able to absorb the $1$ out front by the fact that $(-1)^0/0! = 1$. As a sanity check, with $i = 1$, the answer should be $0$, as the one person will always just grab their hat back, and this does hold here. With $n = 5$, the answer is $$1 - 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{1}{120} = \dfrac{11}{30}$$
hints: Let $H_i$ be the event that person $i$ receives their hat back. We want to compute $\displaystyle \prob{\bigcap_{i=1}^n H_i^c}$, the probability of the event that nobody receives their hat back. The $H_i$ events are clearly not independent, as the knowledge that one person does not receive their hat back automatically implies that someone else can't receive their hat back, as the other person took a hat belonging to a different person. These events are also not disjoint, as it is possible that multiple people do not get their hat back. Therefore, the best approach is to work with the complement, which is to compute the probability at least one person receives their hat back. Since these events are not disjoint, you will need to use the inclusion-exclusion formula.

title: Largest Selector
statement: An urn contains $n$ balls numbered $1, 2, \dots, n$. We select $1 \leq r \leq n$ of then uniformly at random without replacement. Compute the probability that the largest selected number is $1 \leq m \neq n$ when $n = 10, r = 3,$ and $m=7$.
solution: For the maximum to be exactly $m$, we must first fix $m$ within our selection. Afterwards, we must pick $r-1$ of the remaining $m-1$ balls that are at most $m$ without replacement. There are $\binom{m-1}{r-1}$ ways to do this. With no restrictions, there are $\binom{n}{r}$ ways to draw $r$ balls from the population of $n$ without replacement, as the order of drawing is irrelevant. Therefore, the probability of the maximum being exactly $m$ is $$\dfrac{\binom{m-1}{r-1}}{\binom{n}{r}}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{8}$.
hints: For the maximum to be exactly $m$, we must first fix $m$ within our selection. Afterwards, we must pick $r-1$ of the remaining $m-1$ balls that are at most $m$ without replacement.

title: Prime Subset
statement: Suppose that $\Omega = \{1,2,\dots,p\}$, where $p$ is a prime integer. One $\omega \in \Omega$ is selected uniformly at random. Find the number of pairs of subsets $A, B \subseteq \Omega$ such that the events $\{\omega \in A\}$ and $\{\omega \in B\}$ are independent events. Find this when $p = 7$.
solution:
Since the events are independent, we have $P(\omega \in A,\omega \in B) = P(\omega \in A\cap B) = P(\omega \in A)P(\omega \in B)$. Since $\omega$ is selected uniformly at random from $\Omega$, $P(\omega \in A) = \dfrac{|A|}{|\Omega|} = \dfrac{|A|}{p}$, as exactly $|A|$ of the $p$ elements of $\Omega$ are in $A$. Similarly, we have $P(\omega \in B) = \dfrac{|B|}{p}$ and $P(\omega \in A\cap B) = \dfrac{|A\cap B|}{p}$. Setting up the equality from above, we have $$\dfrac{|A\cap B|}{p} = \dfrac{|A|}{p} \cdot \dfrac{|B|}{p} \iff p \cdot |A\cap B| = |A| \cdot |B|$$ Since $p \mid |A| \cdot |B|$, it must be the case that $p \mid |A|$ or $p \mid |B|$. However, as $p$ is prime, the only way this is true is if $|A| = 0$ or $|A| = p$, or likewise with $B$. Therefore, it must be the case that at least one of $A$ or $B$ is either $\emptyset$ or $\Omega$ itself. Thus, we need to find the number of pairs of subsets $(A,B)$ such that at least one of $A$ or $B$ is either $\emptyset$ or $\Omega$. 

$$$$

Note that there are $2^p$ choices for each of $A$ and $B$, as there are $2^p$ subsets of a set of size $p$. Thus, there are $2^p \cdot 2^p = 4^p$ total pairs of subsets. The easiest way to count the number of pairs of interest is via the complement, as the complement is just that neither $A$ nor $B$ is $\emptyset$ nor $\Omega$. This removes $2$ choices for each of $A$ and $B$, leaving $2^p - 2$ options left for each. Thus, there are $(2^p - 2)^2$ pairs of subsets that are not satisfactory, as neither $A$ nor $B$ is $\emptyset$ nor $\Omega$. Thus, $(2^p)^2 - (2^p - 2)^2 = (2^p + (2^p - 2))(2^p - (2^p - 2)) = 2 \cdot (2^{p+1}-2) = 2^{p+2} - 4$ total pairs of subsets $(A,B)$ such that this holds true. With $p = 7$, the answer is $508$.
hints: Since the events are independent, we have $\prob{\omega \in A,\omega \in B} = \prob{\omega \in A\cap B} = \prob{\omega \in A}\prob{\omega \in B}$. Since $\omega$ is selected uniformly at random from $\Omega$, $\prob{\omega \in A} = \dfrac{|A|}{|\Omega|} = \dfrac{|A|}{p}$, as exactly $|A|$ of the $p$ elements of $\Omega$ are in $A$.

title: Random Exam
statement: A student is a taking a multiple choice exam that has $n \geq 2$ choices. The student saw some of the answer key before the exam, so with probability $0 < p < 1$, they know the answer to a given question. If they know the answer, then they always get it correct. If they don't know the answer, the student guesses uniformly at random among the answer choices. Each question has exactly one correct answer. Given that a student got the answer correct, what is the probability that they knew the answer to the question? Answer this when $p = 2/3$ and $n = 6$.
solution:
Let $C$ be the event that the student got the answer correct and $K$ be the event that they knew the answer to the question. We want to compute $P(K \mid C) = \dfrac{P(C \cap K)}{P(C)}$. The student can get the answer correct in two ways: either by knowing the answer or by not knowing the answer and guessing correctly. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether the student knows the answer or not. In particular, we can compute the numerator by $P(C \cap K) = P(C \mid K)P(K)$. The question states that $P(K) = p$ and $P(C \mid K) = 1$, as the student always gets the question correct if they know the answer. 

$$$$

On the denominator, we apply Law of Total Probability to get $P(C) = P(C \mid K)P(K) + P(C \mid K^c)P(K^c)$. The first term is just the numerator. Since $P(K) = p$, by complementation, $P(K^c) = 1 - p$. Given that the student doesn't know the answer, they guess uniformly at random. One of the $n$ answers is correct, so $P(C \mid K^c) = \dfrac{1}{n}$. This means that $$P(K \mid C) = \dfrac{p}{p + 1/n \cdot (1-p)} = \frac{np}{(n-1)p + 1}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{12}{13}$.
hints: Let $C$ be the event that the student got the answer correct and $K$ be the event that they knew the answer to the question. We want to compute $\prob{K \mid C} = \dfrac{\prob{C \cap K}}{\prob{C}}$. The student can get the answer correct in two ways: either by knowing the answer or by not knowing the answer and guessing correctly. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether the student knows the answer or not.

title: Opposite Parity Heads I
statement: We flip a coin that has a probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip $n \geq 2$ times. Given that the first and last flip are of opposite parity, compute the expected number of heads obtained when $p = 3/4$ and $n = 10$.
solution: Let $T$ be the total number of heads in the $n$ flips and $P$ be the event that the first and last flip are of opposite parity. We can write $T = T_1 + T_2$, where $T_1$ is the number of heads obtained in the first and last flip (i.e. restricting to the two flips of interest) and $T_2$ is the number of heads in the remaining $n-2$ flips. The reason we want to do something like this is because the information that we are given says that $T_1 = 1$, as there is one heads and one tails among the first and last flip. In other words, $$E[T \mid P] = E[T_1 + T_2 \mid P] = E[T_1 \mid P] + E[T_2 \mid P] = 1 + E[T_2 \mid P]$$ The number of heads in the remaining $n-2$ flips is independent of the event $P$, as $P$ is only concerned with the first and last flip, while $T_2$ counts the number of heads in the remaining $n-2$ flips. Thus, $E[T_2 \mid P] = E[T_2]$. As $T_2$ counts the number of heads obtained in $n-2$ flips of a coin with probability $p$ of heads per flip, $T_2 \sim \text{Bin}(n-2, p)$. The mean is therefore $E[T_2] = p(n-2)$. This implies $$E[T] = 1 + (n-2)p$$ With the specified values, the answer is $7$.
hints: There must be one head among the first and last flip. The given event does not tell us any information about the remaining $n-2$ flips, so what is the distribution of the number of heads in those flips?

title: Prime Picker
statement: An integer between $2$ and $10$ (inclusive of both) is selected uniformly at random, say $n$. If $n$ is prime, you receive a payout of $\$n$, If $n$ is composite, you pay $\$n/2$. What is the fair value of this game?
solution: The primes at most $10$ are $2,3,5,$ and $7$. For each of these values, the payouts are exactly those values. The composite numbers are $4,6,8,9,$ and $10$. You lose $2,3,4,4.5,$ and $5$ for those outcomes, respectively. Since each of the $9$ values are equally likely to appear, we can just add up the payouts of each outcome to get the expected payout. Namely, we get $$\dfrac{2 + 3 - 2 + 5 - 3 + 7 - 4 - 4.5 - 5}{9} = -\dfrac{1}{6}$$
hints: The primes at most $10$ are $2,3,5,$ and $7$. Compute the expected value via the definition.

title: Factorial Poisson
statement: Let $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. Compute $\mathbb{E}[X!]$ for $0 < \lambda < 1$. Report the answer when $\lambda = 1/2$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution: This expected value doesn't appear to have a nice way to compute it via an alternative method (ex: MGFs, known distributions, etc.), so LOTUS is the best bet here. The PMF of $X \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ is $P(X = k) = \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}$. By LOTUS, we have that $$\mathbb{E}[X!] = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} kP(X=k)= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k! \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!} e^{-\lambda} = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \lambda^k =  \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}}{1-\lambda}$$ The last sum is evaluated by the formula for geometric series. However, for the last calculation to be valid, we need that $\lambda < 1$, as otherwise, the sum diverges to $\infty$. With $\lambda = 1/2$, the answer is approximately $1.213$.
hints: This expected value doesn't appear to have a nice way to compute it via an alternative method (ex: MGFs, known distributions, etc.), so LOTUS is the best bet here.

title: Miami Hurricanes
statement: A family has a sign with the letters MIAMI on the front. A hurricane hits Miami for the $10$th time this year, so two random letters have fallen off this sign. A tourist that isn't from Miami notices this and and glues the letters back up at random. Find the probability that the sign reads MIAMI again.
solution:
If the two letters that fall off are the same, then the sign will always read MIAMI again. However, if they are not the same, it is not guaranteed that the sign will read correctly again. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether the two letters that fell off are the same or not.

$$$$

Let $C$ be the event that the sign is corrected, and $M$ be the event that the two letters that fall off match. The goal is to compute $$P(C) = P(C \mid M)P(M) + P(C \mid M^c)P(M^c)$$ $P(M)$ is just the probability that the two letters that fell off match. There are $5$ letters in MIAMI, so there are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ pairs of letters that could fall off. Of these, $2$ of them are the same letters: $MM$ and $II$. Therefore, $P(M) = 2/10 = 1/5$, which implies $P(M^c) = 1 - 1/5 = 4/5$. 

$$$$

If the letters match, the sign will always be fixed, regardless of how the letters are put back on. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[C \mid M] = 1$. If they do not match, then there is a $50\%$ chance the letters are put back correctly, as there are $2$ ways they can be put back on, and one will be correct, so $P(C \mid M^c) = 1/2$. Plugging this into the Law of Total Probability, $$P(C) = 1 \cdot 1/5 + 1/2 \cdot 4/5 = 3/5$$
hints: If the two letters that fall off are the same, then the sign will always read MIAMI again. However, if they are not the same, it is not guaranteed that the sign will read correctly again. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether the two letters that fell off are the same or not.

title: Ordered Uniforms I
statement: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n \sim U(a, b)$ IID. Define $M_n = \max(X_1,\dots, X_n)$. Compute $E[M_n]$ when $n = 9, a = 5,$ and $b = 15$.
hints: Use the tail integral formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$ with $M_n$. The event $\{M_n \geq x\}$ isn't very conducive to work with, so consider the complement.
Alternatively, use the definition of expected value directly. Use the fact that each $X_{i}$ is independent and the properties of maxima to find the cdf, then differentiate.

title: Auctioneer I
statement: Esubi is selling a rare item called glaciem. She takes one unit of glaciem to an auctioneer. The auctioneer tells her that each person who bids on this piece of glaciem will place a bid (in dollars) that is uniformly distributed in the interval $(a,b)$, and that each bidder will cost $\$p$ to recruit. The highest bidder wins. How many bidders should Esubi recruit to maximize her expected profit when $a = 200, b = 1800,$ and $p = 4$?
solution:
Let $E(n)$ be the expected profit for Esubi when she has $n$ bidders. Our goal is to maximize $E(n)$. Thus, we should find an equation for $E(n)$ first. Afterwards, to maximize this, the idea is to treat $n$ as continuous and set $E'(n) = 0$.

$$$$

The expected profit for Esubi is the expected maximum bid minus the cost of recruiting. The cost of recruiting $n$ people is $np$, as each bidder costs $\$p$ to recruit by the question. The expected maximum bid is really the expected maximum of the $U(a, b)$ random variables. By the result of "Ordered Uniforms I", the answer to this is $a + \dfrac{(b-a)n}{n+1}$. Using this, we have that $$E(n) = a + \dfrac{(b-a)n}{n+1} - np = a + (b-a)\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n+1}\right) - np$$ To maximize this in $n$, we can treat $n$ as continuous, find $E'(n)$, and set $E'(n) = 0$. We can account for $n$ being discrete later.

$$$$

The derivative of $E(n)$ is $E'(n) = \dfrac{b-a}{(n+1)^2} - p$. Setting this equal to $0$, $$\dfrac{b-a}{(n+1)^2} - p = 0 \iff (n+1)^2 = \dfrac{b-a}{p} \iff n = \sqrt{\dfrac{b-a}{p}} - 1$$ In other words, we have that $n^* = \sqrt{\dfrac{b-a}{p}} - 1$ maximizes $E(n)$. However, $n$ is not necessarily continuous, so we must test $\lfloor n^* \rfloor$ and $\lceil n^* \rceil$ to see which results in a larger value of $E(n)$. Whichever one results in a larger value is the optimal value of $n$ that Esubi should select. With the specific values in this question, $n^* = 19$, so $19$ is the answer, as it is integer-valued.
hints: Let $E(n)$ be the expected profit for Esubi when she has $n$ bidders. Find an equation for $E(n)$.
Use the order statistics formula for Uniform random variables.
To maximize $E(n)$, treat $n$ as continuous and set $E'(n) = 0$.

title: Rainbow Ordering
statement: The $7$ letters $ROYGBIV$ are permuted such that all permutations are equally likely. We say that two strings $a_1a_2\dots a_n$ and $b_1b_2\dots b_n$ are equal up to rotation if there exists some integer $0 \leq i \leq n-1$ such that $a_1a_2\dots a_n = b_{i_1}b_{i_2}\dots b_{i_n}$, where $i_k = 1 + (i + k) \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n$. In other words, they are the same strings up to some shift. Find the probability that $ROYGBIV$ and generated permutation are equal up to rotation.
solution:
The idea here is to count the number of distinct strings that there are up to rotation. Once we do that, there is exactly $1$ of those that is $ROYGBIV$ up to rotation.

$$$$

Given a string $a_1a_2\dots a_n$ of all distinct letters, there are exactly $n$ strings that are equivalent to it up to rotation, as each one of the shifts $i = 0,1,\dots, n-1$ yield a distinct string. This is by the assumption that all characters are distinct. Therefore, each string generates $n$ strings that are identical up to rotation, so the number of distinct strings up to rotation is just the total number of strings divided by $n$. There are $n!$ total strings, as there are $n!$ ways to permute the letters, so there are $\frac{n!}{n} = (n-1)!$ strings that are unique up to rotation. Therefore, the answer is $\frac{1}{(n-1)!}$ for a general string of length $n$. Since our string is of length $7$, the answer is $1/720$.
hints: How many distinct strings are there up to rotation? Think of this as a circular permutation problem.

title: Equiside
statement: A coin that has probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip is flipped $n \geq 1$ times. Find the probability that all $n$ flips show the same side when $p = 1/3$ and $n = 5$.
solution: All of the sides can either be all tails or all heads. The events of all $n$ flips being tails/heads are disjoint from each other, so we can disjointify and break up the probability as the sum of the two probabilities that all of the coins are heads and all are tails. There is a probability $p$ per flip that the coin is heads, so the probability all $n$ flips are heads, by independence, is $p^n$. Similarly, the probability that each flip is a tails is $1-p$, so the probability that all $n$ flips are tails is, by independence, $(1-p)^n$. Adding up these two cases, the probability that all of the flips show the same side is $p^n + (1-p)^n$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{33}{243} = \dfrac{11}{81}$.
hints: All of the sides can either be all tails or all heads. Disjointify into these two cases.

title: Prime Roll
statement: A fair standard $6-$sided die is rolled $n \geq 1$ times. Find the probability that exactly $0 \leq k \leq n$ prime integers are rolled when $k = 4$ and $n = 8$.
solution: The prime integers at most $6$ are $2,3,$ and $5$. Thus, $3$ of the $6$ equally likely outcomes per roll are prime, so there is a probability $3/6 = 1/2$ per roll of obtaining a prime integer. We want to find the probability that exactly $k$ prime integers appear in $n$ rolls. As we are looking to count the number of some event that occurs in $n$ independent and identical trials, the binomial distribution is best suited here. Namely, if $N$ counts the number of primes that appear in $n$ rolls, $N \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$. We want to compute $P(N = k)$, the event that there are exactly $k$ primes. Using the PMF of a binomial random variable, $P(N = k) =\displaystyle  \binom{n}{k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^k \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-k} = \binom{n}{k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{70}{256} = \dfrac{35}{128}$.
hints: The prime integers at most $6$ are $2,3,$ and $5$. What distribution does the number of prime integers rolled follow?

title: Acceptance-Rejection Sampling
statement: Suppose that we want to sample from a random variable $X$ with bounded PDF $f(x)$ that is supported on $(0,1)$. One way to do this to sample uniformly at random a pair $(X,Y)$ in the plane from a rectangle $R_h = (0,1) \times (0,h)$ for some $h > 0$. The point $(X,Y)$ will be counted as a valid sample if $(X,Y)$ lies between the $x-$axis and the graph of $f(x)$ in the plane. Otherwise, the sample is considered invalid and is rejected. It can be shown that, for $h$ appropriately selected, $X$ in the pair $(X,Y)$ has marginal PDF $f(x)$. Find the value of $h$ that minimizes the expected number of draws that need to be performed to obtain a valid sample for $X \sim \bet{4}{2}$.
solution:
For a general PDF $f(x)$ that is bounded, we know that the rectangle needs to at least cover the entire graph of the PDF, as we need all parts of the PDF available to be sampled from. Thus, the height of the rectangle must at least be the maximum of the PDF on $(0,1)$. In other words, $h \geq \underset{x \in (0,1)}{\sup f(x)}$. $\underset{x \in (0,1)}{\sup f(x)}$ can essentially be regarded as the "maximum" of the PDF. Intuitively, one may think that $h = \underset{x \in (0,1)}{\sup f(x)}$ would minimize the expected number of draws needed, as it would minimize the amount of "extraneous area" that lies above the curve and still inside the bounding rectangle. This intuition is correct.

$$$$

Namely, if the area of the bounding region is $A$, as $(X,Y)$ is sampled uniformly at random from the region, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The probability that $(X,Y)$ lies under the PDF $f(x)$ is just $1/A$, as the PDF has area $1$ below it by definition, and the total region is of area $A$. Thus, the number of points that would need to be sampled to obtain a valid sample would be $N \sim \geom{1/A}$, as each point independently has probability $1/A$ of being under the curve. Therefore, $E[N] = A$ by the known formulas for a geometric distribution. This directly implies that to minimize the expected number of points that need to be drawn, we must minimize $A$. For this situation, we must have the tightest possible bounding rectangle on the PDF, which means making the height as small as possible that covers all of $f(x)$. The minimum possible height is $\underset{x \in (0,1)}{\sup f(x)}$ by the above discussion, so this indeed proves our intuition correct.

$$$$

For our specific PDF, we must find the maximum of $f(x)$ in $(0,1)$. The PDF of a $\bet{4}{2}$ distribution is $f(x) = 20x^3(1-x)I_{(0,1)}(x)$. To find the maximum, we take the derivative and set it equal to $0$. Namely, $$f'(x) = 20 \cdot (3x^2 - 4x^3) = 0 \iff x = \dfrac{3}{4}$$ Plugging in the maximizer gives us the maximum value. Namely this is $\dfrac{135}{64}$ here, so $h = \dfrac{135}{64}$ is the answer.
hints: For a general PDF $f(x)$ that is bounded, we know that the rectangle needs to at least cover the entire graph of the PDF, as we need all regions to be able to be sampled from under the PDF.
If the area of the region is $A$, what would be the distribution of the number of points that need to be drawn to obtain the first valid one? What does this imply you want to do with the rectangle?

title: Socky Drawer
statement: Miguel takes socks out of his drawer that contains $n \geq 4$ pairs of socks, where each pair has a distinct color. He draws out $2$ socks per day without replacement. Find the probability that the third day Miguel takes out socks is the first day he obtains a matching pair when $n = 6$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
For day $3$ to be the first day that Miguel draws matching socks, he must draw $2$ distinct colored socks in each of the first two days. The probability on day $3$ is dependent on how many remaining pairs are left in the drawer by that point. The number of pairs left is directly determined by what Miguel does on day $2$, as there are a couple of cases:

\begin{itemize}
    \item WLOG, say on day $1$ that Miguel picks $2$ socks of colors $1$ and $2$. Miguel could pick the other socks of colors $1$ and $2$, leaving $n-2$ complete colors (both socks of the color are in).
    \item Miguel could pick one of colors $1$ or $2$, and a sock of another color, say $3$, leaving $n-3$ complete colors and $2$ colors with one sock.
    \item Miguel could pick two socks of colors $3$ and $4$ on the second day, leaving $n-4$ complete pairs and $4$ pairs with $1$ sock each.
\end{itemize}

Due to this dependence on what happens in day $2$, the best thing to do is to condition on the number of pairs that overlap between days $1$ and $2$ in Miguel's selection.

$$$$

The two color selections in day $1$ are irrelevant: No pairs have been selected yet, and all the colors are arbitrary, so as long as he removes $2$ distinct color socks, we are good. Regardless of which color Miguel draws for the first of the pair, $2n-2$ of the remaining $2n-1$ socks are not the same as the first. Therefore, the probability that he selects distinct colors on the first day is $\frac{2n-2}{2n-1}$. There will now be $n-2$ complete pairs of socks in the drawer, as well as $2$ singleton socks. 

$$$$

Let $M$ be the event that day $3$ is the first day that Miguel draws matching socks, and $O_i, i = 0,1,2$, be the events that Miguel draws $i$ sock colors in common between days $1$ and $2$. By the Law of Total Probability, $$P(M) = P(M \mid O_0)P(O_0) +P(M \mid O_1)P(O_1) + P(M \mid O_2)P(O_2)$$ In these types of problems, computing the probability that there is complete overlap and complete disjointness is typically easiest. Note that there are $\binom{2n-2}{2}$ ways to draw $2$ socks on day $2$, as there are $2n-2$ socks that remain in the drawer. Exactly $1$ of those pairs are the same colors as day $1$, as only $1$ of each of those colors remain in the drawer. The above implies that $$ P(O_2) = \dfrac{1}{\binom{2n-2}{2}} \hspace{20pt}$$ As for $P(O_0)$, we can't have either sock overlap in color with the ones from the first day. We will consider this part with ordering for now, and then remove ordering later. This is reasonable because the first sock of the pair selected puts additional constraints on the second sock. There are $2n-4$ socks that are not of the colors of the socks from day $1$. Once that sock is selected, there are $2n-6$ socks remaining that can be selected that are none of the prior colors, as we want no match. Then, we must divide by $2$ to remove the ordering of the selection above. This implies $$P(O_0) = \dfrac{\frac{(2n-4)(2n-6)}{2}}{\binom{2n-2}{2}}$$ We want to remove ordering because we ignored ordering in the first computations. We can't just do $\binom{2n-4}{2}$ because that would allow us to select any two socks from the remaining $2n-4$, of which some of those are pairs of the same color.

$$$$

As for the event of one overlap, we can do this without ordering directly. There are $2$ ways to pick the color of the sock that overlaps with one of the colors from the first day, and then $2n-4$ ways to pick the color of the order sock, since it can be any of the socks that aren't the first. This already disregards the order of selection, so we can conclude $$P(O_1) = \dfrac{2(2n-4)}{\binom{2n-2}{2}}$$ Note that $P(O_0) + P(O_1) + P(O_2) \neq 1$ because there is positive probability of selecting matching socks on the second day. Now, we compute the conditional probabilities for each case. If the sock colors drawn in days $1$ and $2$ are both the same, there are still $n-2$ pairs of socks left. Thus, there are $n-2$ pairs of socks for day $3$ that can be drawn out of $\binom{2n-4}{2}$ possible pairs of socks that could be drawn. Therefore, $P(M \mid O_2) = \dfrac{n-2}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$.

$$$$

By the same logic as above, if there is $1$ sock color overlap between the first two days, one additional sock color was removed, so there are $n-3$ pairs of socks that remain. As there are still $2n-4$ total socks left to pick from, $P(M \mid O_1) = \dfrac{n-3}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$. Lastly, if all $4$ socks drawn in the first two days are different colors, then there are $n-4$ pairs of socks that remain, so there are $n-4$ pairs of socks that can be drawn on the last day that are of the same color, meaning $P(M \mid O_0) = \dfrac{n-4}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$. Plugging all of these into Law of Total Probability, $$P(M) = \dfrac{(n-4) \cdot \frac{(2n-4)(2n-6)}{2} + (n-3) \cdot 2(2n-4) + (n-2) \cdot 1}{\binom{2n-2}{2}\binom{2n-4}{2}}$$ With the specific value of $n$, the answer is $\approx 0.072$.
hints: For day $3$ to be the first day that Miguel draws matching socks, he must draw distinct colors for each of the first two days. The probability on day $3$ is dependent on how many remaining pairs are left in the drawer by that point. The number of pairs left is directly determined by what Miguel does on day $2$, as he could pick out the same colors as day $1$ and not reduce the number of remaining pairs, or he could pick the other extreme of selecting $2$ sock colors that haven't been seen yet, reducing the number of remaining pairs by $2$. Thus, the best thing to do is to condition on the number of pairs that overlap between days $1$ and $2$ in Miguel's selection.

title: Point Walker
statement: A uniformly random walker starts at position $k > 0$, where $k$ is an integer. Each step, the walker moves to position $k+1$ or $k-1$ with equal probability. Find the probability that the walker hits position $0$ before position $n > k$. Solve this when $k = 10$ and $n = 25$.
solution: We can view this problem in the same light as Gambler's Ruin, where moving to $k+1$ from $k$ is a win and to $k-1$ is a loss. Therefore, this question is really asking to find the probability that the gambler ruins before hitting $\$n$ when they currently have $\$k$. This is just $1 - \dfrac{k}{n}$ by the result of "Gambler's Ruin I". With the specific values, the answer is just $3/5$.
hints: We can view this problem in the same light as Gambler's Ruin, where moving to $k+1$ from $k$ is a win and to $k-1$ is a loss.

title: Driving the Boat
statement: Ahoy! Spongebob asks to drive the boat. However, he is very poor at being a captain, so he crashes the ship on an island. The probability that a rescue boat passes by in the next hour is $p$. Assuming that boat arrivals are memoryless, find the probability that a boat passes by in the next $m$ minutes, where $m \mid 60$? Solve this for $m = 15$ and $p = 0.9744$.
solution: The probability that a boat does not arrive in the next hour is $1-p$. The reason to use the complement here is that the event of a boat not arriving is easier to relate to what happens in each of the individual time intervals. If a boat doesn't arrive in the next hour, then there is no boat in each of the $60/m$ $m$ minute intervals. By the memorylessness of arrivals, boats arrive in each time interval independently. Thus, if $p_m$ is the probability of a boat arriving in a given $m$ minute time interval, $(1-p_m)^{60/m}$ is the probability that a boat does not arrive within any of the $60/m$ $m$ minute time intervals, as $1-p_m$ is the probability that it does not arrive for each independent time interval. With this, we can now equate $$(1-p_m)^{60/m} = 1-p \iff 1-p_m = (1-p)^{m/60} \iff p_m = 1 - (1-p)^{m/60}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $0.6$.
hints: The probability that a boat does not arrive in the next hour is $1-p$. If a boat doesn't arrive in the next hour, then there is no boat in each of the $60/m$ $m-$minute intervals. By the memorylessness of arrivals, boats arrive in each time interval independently.

title: Point Picker I
statement: Fix $1 \leq r \leq n$. Andy and Barry are selecting uniformly random $r-$element subsets from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Find the probability that Andy and Barry select the same subset when $r = 4$ and $n = 8$.
solution: The key here is to fix Andy's subset arbitrarily, as all subsets are equally likely to be selected from $[n]$. In other words, given that Andy and Barry select the same subset, it is equally likely to be any of the possible subsets, so it doesn't matter which one Andy picks. There are $\binom{n}{r}$ total subsets of size $r$ of $[n]$ that Barry can pick for his subset, of which exactly $1$ of them is Andy's subset.
