hints: Since the subset is selected uniformly at random from all subsets of size $k$, we can compute the probability by taking the ratio of the number of subsets of size $k$ that satisfy the condition to the total number of subsets of size $k$. How many total subsets of size $k$ are there? How many of those include $1$?

title: Different Intersection I
statement: Fix $0 \leq a,b \leq n$. Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $[n]$ that are independently and uniformly at random selected from the collection of subsets of sizes $a$ and $b$, respectively. Find $E[|A\cap B|]$ when $a = 6, b = 8,$ and $n = 12$.
solution:
There is no clear way to proceed in this problem by deriving the PMF of $|A \cap B|$, so an alternative must be better. Note that the number of elements in $|A\cap B|$ is just the sum of indicators that represent whether or not each element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. Therefore, the best approach is to use linearity of expectation on indicators. 

$$$$

In particular, let $I_i$ be the indicator that element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. We set up the indicators this way so that we can count the expected number of elements in $A \cap B$. Therefore, we have that $|A\cap B| = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total number of elements in $A\cap B$. As the two subsets are selected uniformly at random from the subsets of those respective sizes, each element has the same probability of being included in $A$, and likewise with $B$. Therefore, the indicators are all exchangeable, and hence have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, we have $$E[|A \cap B|] = nE[I_1]$$ $E[I_1]$ is the probability that $1$ is in $A \cap B$. Since $A$ are $B$ are selected independently, we have that $P(1 \in A \cap B) = P(1 \in A)P(1 \in B)$. By the result of "Include The Element!", as $|A| = a$ and $|B| = b$, $P(1 \in A) = \dfrac{a}{n}$ and $P(1 \in B) = \dfrac{b}{n}$. Plugging these in, we get $$E[|A\cap B|] = n \cdot \dfrac{a}{n} \cdot \dfrac{b}{n} = \dfrac{ab}{n}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $4$.
hints: There is no clear way to proceed in this problem by deriving the PMF of $|A \cap B|$, so an alternative must be better. Note that the number of elements in $|A\cap B|$ is just the sum of indicators that represent whether or not each element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. Therefore, use linearity of expectation on appropriately selected indicators.

title: Modular Pairs
statement: What is the minimum number of pairs of integers $(a,b)$ that are needed to guarantee that there exist two pairs $(a_1,b_1)$ and $(a_2,b_2)$ such that $a_1 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n = a_2 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n$ and $b_1 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n = b_2 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n$, where $n \geq 2$ is an integer? Solve this when $n = 7$.
solution: Note that there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that $a_1$ and $a_2$ both belong to. Similarly, there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that both $b_1$ and $b_2$ belong to. Therefore, by the multiplication principle, there are $n^2$ total ways to pick the pair of equivalence classes that the $a_i$s and the $b_i$s belong to. By the Pigeonhole Principle, if there are at least $n^2 + 1$ pairs, there must exist two pairs that satisfy the above, as there are only $n^2$ pigeonholes (pairs of equivalence classes). With less than $n^2 + 1$ pairs, it is possible that no two belong to the same pigeonhole, so $n^2 + 1$ is the absolute minimum. With the specified value here, the answer is $50$.
hints: How many choices are there for the equivalence class of the $a_i$? Similar for the $b_i$?

title: Conditional Values
statement: Suppose that $X$ is a discrete random variable with positive integer support. Fix a subset $B \subseteq \Z^+$. For any $i \in Z^+ \setminus B$, compute $P(X = i \mid X \notin B)$ when $X \sim \geom{1/2}, B = \{1,2,\dots, 10\}$, and $i = 12$.
solution:
Since we are looking to compute a conditional probability here, it's best to first apply the definition of conditional probability! Applying the definition and reducing yields $$P(X = i \mid X 
otin B) = \dfrac{P(X = i, X 
otin B)}{P(X 
otin B)} = \dfrac{P(X = i)}{P(X 
otin B)}$$ The top reduces because it is already assumed that $i 
otin B$, so if $X = i$, $X 
otin B$ automatically. The top is already reduced as can be. As for the bottom, we can evaluate $P(X 
otin B)$ by summing over the PMF of $X$ for all $i 
otin B$. Namely, $P(X 
otin B) = \displaystyle \sum_{i \in \Z^+ \setminus B} P(X = i)$. Plugging this in, the result is $$P(X = i \mid X 
otin B) = \dfrac{P(X = i)}{\sum_{i \in \Z^+ \setminus B} P(X = i)}$$ With the specified values, $P(X = 12) = 2^{-12}$, while $P(X 
otin B) = P(X > 10) = 2^{-10}$, as $\{X > 10\}$ is exactly the event that the first $10$ flips of a fair coin are tails. Therefore, our answer is $1/4$.
hints: Consider using the definition of conditional probability here and sum up over the values in the support.

title: Tuple Birthdays
statement: There are $n$ people in a probability class. Each person is equally likely to be born on any day of the $365$ days in a year. Compute the expected number of groups of $2 \leq k \leq n$ people that have the same birthday when $n = 25$ and $k = 4$. Round to the nearest hundred-thousandth.
solution:
In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected number of $k-$subsets of people that have the same birthdays. Therefore, we should set up indicators that indicate whether each $k-$subset of people have the same birthday or not. There are $\binom{n}{k}$ such subsets of $k$ people. Label the $k-$subsets $1$ to $\binom{n}{k}$ arbitrarily, and let $I_{i}$ be the indicator of the event that $k-$subset $i$ all shares the same birthday. By the above discussion, $\displaystyle T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{k}}$ gives the total number of $k-$subsets of people sharing a birthday. Since the labels for the $k-$subsets are arbitrary, the random variables are all exchangeable, meaning they all have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, $$E[T] = \binom{n}{k}E[I_{1]}$$ 

$$$$

Now, $E[I_{1]}$ is just the probability that the people in the $k-$subset labeled $1$ all have the same birthday. Since the labels are arbitrary, suppose the people in this group are labelled $1$ to $k$. Since all days are equally likely, fix the birthday of person $1$ arbitrarily. There is a $1/365$ chance that each of the other $k-1$ people have the same birthday as person $1$, as there is $1$ day of the year that matches the birthday of person $1$. Since each person is independent, the probability all $k$ people share the same birthday is $E[I_1] = 365^{-(k-1)}$. Plugging this in above, $$E[T] = \dfrac{1}{365^{k-1}}\binom{n}{k}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.00026$.
hints: Define an indicator random variable that is equal to 1 if all of the people in a particular subset all have the same birthday. Then, use the linearity of expectation.

title: Ice Cream Orders
statement: An ice cream store sells cups and cones. A cup can hold small, medium, and large scoops, while a cone can only hold small and medium scoops. There are $8$ cup toppings and $12$ cone toppings. How many one-topping ice cream orders are there?
solution:
The size of the ice cream order allowed is dependent on whether a cone or cup is selected. Therefore, it's best to break up this problem into two cases: Cone and cup. These cases are disjoint (you can't have both a cone and cup) and exhaustive (every ice cream order uses either a cone or cup). 

$$$$

For the cup case, there are $3$ size options and $8$ toppings, meaning there are $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ ice cream options with a cup. For a cone, there are only $2$ sizes and $12$ toppings, so there are $2 \cdot 12 = 24$ ice cream options with a cone. Adding these together, we have $48$ total orders.
hints: The size of the ice cream order allowed is dependent on whether a cone or cup is selected. Therefore, it's best to break up this problem into two cases: Cone and cup.

title: NASCAR Results
statement: $100$ cars in NASCAR are racing. Each car is designated a distinct number $0-99$. Find the number of outcomes that have all $10$ cars of single-digit label finishing together (For example, cars $0-9$ finish in the top 10 or in places $52-61$). The answer is in the form $a!b!$ for some integers $a$ and $b$. Report $ab$.
solution:
To count the number of outcomes satisfying this, we must first select the $10$ spots for which all $10$ of the single-digit cars will reside in. Note that the spot of the first single-digit car locks in the spots for the other $9$ single-digit label cars. They can start as early as the first spot or as late as the $91$st spot, as that would be the last $10$ spots. Thus, there are $91$ ways to pick the $10$ spots of the single-digit cars. Then, once those spots are selected, there are $10!$ ways to arrange the $10$ single-digit label cars on those $10$ spots. Lastly, there are $90!$ ways to arrange the other $90$ cars on the remaining $90$ spots. Thus, by the multiplication principle, there are $91 \cdot 10! \cdot 90! = 10!91!$ outcomes that satisfy this condition. 

Alternatively, we could treat the $10$ single-digit cars as a "block", as they must finish together. The other $90$ cars still exist and are distinct. Thus, we have $91$ items we must order: the block and the other $90$ cars. There are $91!$ ways to arrange all of these items. Then, inside the block, the $10$ cars can finish in $10!$ different ways, as we are permuting the $10$ cars inside the block to the $10$ spots inside of it, so the number of satisfactory outcomes is $10!91!$.
hints: To count the number of outcomes satisfying this, first select the $10$ spots for which all $10$ of the single-digit cars will reside in. Note that the spot of the first single-digit car locks in the spots for the other $9$ single-digit label cars.

title: Modified Full House I
statement: How many $5-$card hands from a standard $52-$card deck consist of $2$ cards of one suit and $3$ cards of another suit?
solution:
The first thing we need to ask ourselves is: Does the ordering of suits matter? The answer is yes because we are selecting only $2$ of one, but $3$ of the other, so if we swap the two suits around, we do indeed get a different full house. Thus, we first have to permute $k=2$ suits from $n=4$ total suits in the deck, as which suit receives $3$ cards vs. $2$ cards matters. There are $P(4,2)$ ways to do this. 

$$$$

For the suit that has $3$ replicates in the hand, the order of the cards selected is irrelevant, so we want a subset of size $k = 3$ from a set of $n = 13$ cards of that suit, which can be selected in $\binom{13}{3}$ ways. Then, for the suit with $2$ replicates, by the same logic, there are $\binom{13}{2}$ ways to pick $2$ cards from the other suit. By the multiplication principle, the answer is $$\displaystyle P(4,2)\cdot \binom{13}{3} \cdot \binom{13}{2} = 267696$$
hints: The first thing we need to ask ourselves is: Does the ordering of suits matter?
The answer is yes because we are selecting only $2$ of one, but $3$ of the other, so if we swap the two suits around, we do indeed get a different full house.

title: Special Term
statement: Determine the coefficient of $x^{25}y^{50}$ when expanding $(2x-y)^{75}$. The answer can be written in the form $a \cdot 10^b$ in scientific notation. Report the answer of $a + b$, rounded to the nearest hundredth.
solution: We can write $(2x-y)^{75} = (2x+ (-y))^{75}$, so by applying the binomial theorem with $2x, -y,$ and $75$, we obtain $$(2x-y)^{75} = \sum_{k=0}^{75} \binom{75}{k}(2x)^k(-y)^{75 - k} = \sum_{k=0}^{75}\binom{75}{k}2^k(-1)^{75-k} x^ky^{75-k}$$ We get $x^{25}y^{50} = x^{25}y^{75-25}$ when $k = 25$. Plugging in $k =25$, we get the term $$\binom{75}{25}(2x)^{25}(-y)^{50} = 2^{25}\binom{75}{25}x^{25}y^{50}$$ Therefore, $\displaystyle 2^{25}\binom{75}{25} \approx 1.76 \cdot 10^{27}$ is the coefficient. The answer is $28.76$.
hints: We can write $(2x-y)^{75} = (2x+ (-y))^{75}$. Apply the binomial theorem.

title: Binomial Coefficient Difference
statement: Find an expression, potentially dependent on $n$, for $\displaystyle \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n, \hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{even}} \binom{n}{k} - \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n,\hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{odd}} \binom{n}{k}$. Evaluate this when $n = 20$.
solution: In this, we see a sum and difference of binomial coefficients, so we should instantly think to use the binomial theorem. We can condense the two sums into one because all that changes is the sign for even vs. odd. Doing this, $$\sum_{0 \leq k \leq n, \hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{even}} \binom{n}{k} - \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n,\hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{odd}} \binom{n}{k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(-1)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(-1)^k1^{n-k} = (-1 + 1)^n = 0$$ We are able to condense the two sums into one by noting that all the terms with even $k$ are positive, while those with odd $k$ are negative. Lastly, we applied the binomial theorem with $x = -1$ and $y = 1$. Since this holds for all $n$, the answer is $0$.
hints: Can you somehow condense this difference into one sum?

title: Diego's Exam
statement: Diego is randomly answering questions on a multiple choice test with $10$ questions. Each question has $4$ answer choices, of which $1$ is correct. He selects uniformly at random for each question. Find the probability that Diego gets at least $2$ questions correct on this exam. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Since this an "at least" probability involving separate questions (his answers to previous questions don't influence his answers to future questions), the complementary rule is best to apply. 

$$$$

Let $A$ be the event that Diego correctly answers at least $2$ questions. $A^c$ is the event that he answers either $0$ or $1$ question correctly, as these outcomes ensure Diego did not answer at least $2$ questions correctly. Since we are looking at the number of correct answers in Diego's exam and we know each sequence of answers to the $10$ questions are equally likely, we should set up the sample space as all possible sequences of $10$ answers that Diego can submit. 

$$$$

Each answer has $4$ options, so there are $4^{10}$ possible ways to answer the exam. The events of obtaining exactly $0$ correct answers and exactly $1$ correct answer are disjoint events. Therefore, if we let $C_0$ and $C_1$ be the events that Diego gets $0$ and $1$ questions correct, respectively, $A^c = C_0 \cup C_1$. By finite disjoint additivity, $$\mathbb{P}[A^c] = \mathbb{P}[C_0] + \mathbb{P}[C_1]$$ $\mathbb{P}[C_0]$ is the probability he selects a wrong answer for all $10$ questions. There are $3$ wrong answers per question of the $4$ questions, so there are $|C_0| = 3^{10}$ ways he can answer every question wrong. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[C_0] = 3^{10}/4^{10}$. $\mathbb{P}[C_1]$ is the probability that Diego gets exactly $1$ question right. There are $10$ ways to pick the answer he gets correct. For that question, there is only one right answer. For the other $9$ questions, there are $3$ ways to pick a wrong answer. By the multiplication rule, there are $|C_1| = 10 \cdot 1 \cdot 3^9 = 10 \cdot 3^9$ ways to get one answer correct. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[C_1] = 10 \cdot 3^9 / 4^{10}$. Substituting back in, we have that $$\mathbb{P}[A^c] = \dfrac{3^{10} + 10 \cdot 3^9}{4^{10}} \iff P(A) = 1 - P(A^c) = 1 - \dfrac{3^{10} + 10 \cdot 3^9}{4^{10}}$$
hints: Since this an "at least" probability involving separate questions (his answers to previous questions don't influence his answers to future questions), the complementary rule is best to apply.

title: Uniformly Random Permutation Formed, Fixed
statement: Fix $n \geq 2$. A uniformly random permutation $f: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ is being formed, where $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. We say that $1 \leq i \leq n$ is fixed if $f(i) = i$. When $n = 10$, find the probability that $1$ is fixed, but $2$ is not fixed.
solution:
Let's first convert this statement into the language of events. For each $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $F_i$ be the event that $i$ is a fixed point. We are looking to compute $P(F_1 \cap F_2^c)$, as we want $1$ fixed and $2$ not fixed. To compute a probability of this form, we can use the corollary of the differencing property above. We can write $$P(F_1 \cap F_2^c) + P(F_1 \cap F_2) = P(F_1) \iff P(F_1 \cap F_2^c) = P(F_1) - P(F_1 \cap F_2)$$ More simply, we consider all outcomes where $1$ is fixed, and then remove the outcomes where $2$ is also fixed. In this question, we know all permutations are equally likely, so we should consider the sample space to be all permutations of $[n]$. There are $n!$ total permutations without restrictions, as $[n]$ has size $n$. Now, we must compute $|F_1|$ and $|F_1 \cap F_2|$. For $|F_1|$, we first fix $1$, and then we permute the other $n-1$ elements in any order, as there are no other restrictions. Thus, there are $|F_1| = (n-1)!$ permutations for this case. For $|F_1 \cap F_2|$, we fix $1$ and $2$, and there we permute the other $n-2$ elements in any order. Thus, there are $|F_1 \cap F_2| = (n-2)!$ permutations for this case. By the equally likely model, $P(F_1) = \frac{(n-1)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n}$ and $P(F_1 \cap F_2) = \frac{(n-2)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}$. Substituting these into the differencing formula, $$P(F_1 \cap F_2^c) = \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} = \frac{n-2}{n(n-1)}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $4/45$.

We can alternatively just directly compute this via combinatorics. There are $n(n-1)$ ways to assign $1$ and $2$ to $f(1)$ and $f(2)$, as they can't map to the same value. If $1$ is fixed, $f(1) = 1$ is the only option. If $2$ is not fixed, $f(2)$ can be any value besides $1$ and $2$. Thus, there are $n-2$ options for where $2$ maps to, meaning that the probability of the event is $$\dfrac{n-2}{n(n-1)}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $4/45$.
hints: For each $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $F_i$ be the event that $i$ is a fixed point. We are looking to compute $\prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c}$, as we want $1$ fixed and $2$ not fixed.

title: Powerball Winner II
statement: A lottery consists of $6$ values. The first $5$ values are distinct integers $1-69$, inclusive. The last value is the Powerball number, which is a value $1-26$, inclusive. The Powerball number can match one of the other $5$ values. One wins the lottery by matching all $6$ values. The order of the first $5$ values is irrelevant. All tickets are equally likely to be generated and can be generated multiple times. Suppose that you purchase $2$ lottery tickets once a week for the next $60$ years of your life. This means you purchase approximately $6240$ tickets. Find the probability you win the lottery at least once in the next $60$ years. If $q$ is the probability, report the answer of $q \cdot 10^5$, rounded to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Label the tickets $1-6240$, and let $T_i$ be the event that ticket $i$ is a winning ticket. Then we want $\mathbb{P}[T_1 \cup T_2 \dots \cup T_{6240}]$, the probability that at least one is a winning ticket. Since each ticket is generated randomly, we can assume each of these events are independent, so $$P(\bigcup_{i=1)^{6240} T_i} = 1 - P(\bigcap_{i=1)^{6240} T_i^c}$$ By the independence of the $T_i$ events, their complements must also be independent. Therefore, the above is $P(\bigcup_{i=1)^{6240} T_i} = 1 - \mathbb{P}[T_1^c]\dots \mathbb{P}[T_{6240}^c] = 1 - (1 - \mathbb{P}[T_1])\dots (1 - \mathbb{P}[T_{6240}])$. Since each of the tickets is randomly generated, they all have the same probability of being a winning ticket, which we found in "Powerball Winner I" to be about $3.422 \cdot 10^{-9}$. Thus, this probability is $$P(\bigcup_{i=1)^{6240} T_i} = 1 - (1 - 3.422 \cdot 10^{-9})^{6240} \approx 2.135 \cdot 10^{-5}$$ The answer to this question is $2.135$.
hints: Label the tickets $1-6240$, and let $T_i$ be the event that ticket $i$ is a winning ticket. Then we want $\mathbb{P}[T_1 \cup T_2 \dots \cup T_{6240}]$, the probability that at least one is a winning ticket.

title: Disease Prevalence I
statement: The prevalence of a disease within a population is $1\%$. A test for the disease is created. If the person has the disease, there is a $99\%$ chance they test positive. If they don't have the disease, there is still a false positive rate of $3\%$. Find the probability a person actually has the disease if they test positive.
solution:
In this question, we have two groups of people. Namely, they are infected and healthy individuals. Thus, one can have the disease by either obtaining a positive or negative test. This observation yields the natural choice of conditioning on whether the test is positive or negative.

\nl

Let $D$ denote an individual with the disease and $+$ denote an individual that tests positive. We have that $\mathbb{P}[D] = 0.01$, $\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D] = 0.99$, and $\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D^c] = 0.03$ from the question. We want $\mathbb{P}[D \mid +]$, the probability a person who receives a positive test has the disease. By the definition of conditional probability, this is $$P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[D+]}{\mathbb{P}[+]}$$ By conditioning on whether or not the person has the disease, we have that $$\mathbb{P}[D \mid +] = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D]\mathbb{P}[D]}{\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D]\mathbb{P}[D] + \mathbb{P}[+ \mid D^c]\mathbb{P}[D^c]}$$ Note that $\mathbb{P}[D^c] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[D] = 0.99$. Plugging all values in, we get that $$\mathbb{P}[D \mid +] = \dfrac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.03 \cdot 0.99} = \dfrac{1}{4}$$ This probability is very low. This is because the number of false positives arising in the general population outweighs the true positives themselves.
hints: In this question, we have two groups of people. Namely, they are infected and healthy individuals. Thus, one can have the disease by either obtaining a positive or negative test. This observation yields the natural choice of conditioning on whether the test is positive or negative.

title: Bertrand's Box
statement: Two boxes are in front of you. One box has a $\$100$ bill and a $\$1$ bill, while the other has $2$ $\$100$ bills. You pick a box at random and then pick a bill from it at random without replacement. It is an $\$100$ bill. Find the probability you select a second $\$100$ on the next draw.
solution:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ denote the boxes with $1$ and $2$ $\$100$ bills, respectively, and let $E$ be the event that you select an $\$100$ bill on your first draw. The probability of selecting two $\$100$ bills is dependent on what box you chose from. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the box of choice.

$$$$

If you are to select a second $\$100$ bill, then you must be in box $2$, as you select without replacement. Given that you are in box $2$, you must select a $\$100$ bill, whereas it's not possible if you are in box $1$, so we want to compute $$\mathbb{P}[B_2 \mid E] = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[B_2E]}{\mathbb{P}[E]}$$ The numerator is just $\mathbb{P}[B_2E] = \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2]\mathbb{P}[B_2]$. For the denominator, we condition on what box we are in. The denominator becomes $\mathbb{P}[E] = \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_1]\mathbb{P}[B_1] + \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2]\mathbb{P}[B_2]$. We know $\mathbb{P}[B_1] = \mathbb{P}[B_2] = \dfrac{1}{2}$ because we choose at random. If we are in Box 1, it is equally likely whether or not you get an $\$100$ bill on the first draw, so $\mathbb{P}[E \mid B_1] = \dfrac{1}{2}$. If we are in Box 2, you are guaranteed an $\$100$ bill, so $\mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2] = 1$. Plugging this in, we get $\mathbb{P}[B_2 \mid E] = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1}{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ after reduction. Note that there are $3$ $\$100$ bills between the two boxes, of which two of them belong to box $2$. Thus, it should make intuitive sense that if you draw a $\$100$ bill out, there is a probability $2/3$ that it was drawn from box $2$.
hints: Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ denote the boxes with $1$ and $2$ $\$100$ bills, respectively, and let $E$ be the event that you select an $\$100$ bill on your first draw. The probability of selecting two $\$100$ bills is dependent on what box you chose from. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the box of choice.

title: Multisocks
statement: Suppose you have $k \geq 1$ drawers with $r \geq 1$ distinct colors of socks. In drawer $i$, there are $n_{ij}$ socks of color $j$, where $1 \leq i \leq k$ and $1 \leq j \leq r$. One drawer is selected uniformly at random, and a sock from that drawer is selected uniformly at random. The sock is of color $1 \leq j \leq r$. Find the probability that you selected from drawer $i$. Solve this when $k = 3, r = 3, i = 2, j = 2$ and $n_{ij} = i+j$
solution:
The probability that you drawer a sock of color $j$ from a drawer depends on which drawer you selected from, as they each have different proportions of each color of sock. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the drawer number that was selected. Let $D_i$ be the event that drawer $i$ was selected, and let $S_j$ be the event that a sock of color $j$ was selected. We want to compute $P(D_i \mid S_j)$, as we know a sock of color $j$ was selected. To do this, we first use the conditional probability formula $$P(D_i \mid S_j) = \dfrac{P(D_i \cap S_j)}{P(S_j)}$$

On the numerator, we switch the direction of the conditional to obtain $P(D_i \cap S_j)  = P(S_j \mid D_i)P(D_i)$. Since the drawer is selected uniformly at random from the $k$ drawers, $P(D_i) = 1/k$ for each $i$. Given that drawer $i$ was selected, there are $n_{ij}$ total socks of color $j$ in drawer $i$, and there are a total of $\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}$ socks in drawer $i$, as we sum over the amounts of socks of each type. Therefore, we obtain $$P(S_j \mid D_i) = \dfrac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}$$ On the numerator, we play the same game, but we condition on the drawer of selection. This yields $$P(S_j) = \sum_{i=1}^k P(S_j \mid D_i)P(D_i) = \dfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k \dfrac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}$$ Plugging all of these in, $$P(D_i \mid S_j) = \dfrac{\frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{i=1}^r n_{ij}}}{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}}$$ In other words, the probability is the proportion of socks of type $j$ in drawer $i$ divided by the sum of the proportions among all drawers. With the specified values, the answer is $1/3$.

title: Sample Space Reduction
statement: Let $B$ be a non-empty set with $|B| = n$, and let $A \subseteq B$ with $|A| = k$, where $0 \leq k \leq n$. A uniformly random element of $B$ is selected. For any $b \in B\setminus A$, compute the probability $b$ is selected given that the chosen element is not in $A$. Solve this when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution:
For notation, let $x$ be the element selected from $B$. We are given that $x 
otin A$, and we want to compute the probability $x = b$. In other words, we must compute $$P(x = b \mid x 
otin A) = \dfrac{P(x = b, x 
otin A)}{P(x 
otin A)}$$ Since $x 
otin A$ by definition, $P(x = b, x 
otin A) = P(x = b) = 1/n$ by the uniformity of the selected element from $B$. Now, since the selected element is uniformly at random and $|A| = k$, the probability that $x \in A$ is $k/n$, as it contains $k$ of the $n$ equally likely elements. Thus, $P(x 
otin A) = 1 - k/n$. Plugging these in yields $$P(x = b \mid x 
otin A) = \dfrac{1/n}{1-k/n} = \dfrac{1}{n-k}$$ This result makes a lot of intuitive sense: If we know that the selected element is not in $A$, we remove $k$ possibilities from being selected, and then there are now $n-k$ equally likely elements remaining that can be selected. This means that the conditional probability of selecting any of these elements is just $ rac{1}{n-k}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/6$.

otin A} = \dfrac{\prob{x = b, x 
otin A}}{\prob{x 
otin A}}$$

title: Discrete-Time Memorylessness
statement: Suppose $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$. For positive integers $r$ and $s$, compute $\mathbb{P}[X > r + s \mid X > r]$. Report the answer when $p = 1/3, r = 5,$ and $s = 3$.
solution:
To compute this probability, it would know how to compute unconditional probabilities of the form $P(X > x)$, where $x$ is an integer. The event $\{X \leq x\}$ means that the first heads appears in the first $x$ flips. In other words, there is at least one head in the first $x$ flips. However, as this is an "at least one" statement, it's typically easier to consider the complement. In particular, the complement would be the event $\{X > x\}$ i.e. it takes more than $x$ flips to see the first heads. This would mean that all of the first $x$ flips are tails. The probability that all of the first $x$ flips are tails is $(1-p)^x$, as each flip is independent. Therefore, $P(X > x) = (1-p)^x$. By complementation, we have $$P(X \leq x) = 1 - P(X > x) = 1 - (1-p)^x$$

$$$$

In this question, there is a conditional probability. Thus, the best first step is to use the definition of conditional probability. Namely, $$P(X > r+s \mid X > r) = \dfrac{P(X > r+s, X> r)}{P(X > r)}$$ If $X > r+s$, then $X > r$ automatically, as $r+s$ is larger than $r$. Thus, $\{X > r+s\} \subseteq \{X > r\}$, so $P(X > r+s,X>r) = P(X > r+s) = (1-p)^{r+s}$. The denominator, by letting $x = r$, is $P(X > r) = (1-p)^r$. Plugging these in, we get $$P(X > r+s \mid X > r) = \dfrac{(1-p)^{r+s}}{(1-p)^r} = (1-p)^s = P(X > s)$$

$$$$

What does this result intuitively mean and why does it make sense? This statement essentially says: Given that all of the first $r$ flips are tails, the probability that all of the first $r+s$ flips are tails is equal to the probability that $s$ flips are tails. This makes intuitive sense, as if the first $r$ flips are all tails, $s$ additional flips need to be tails for the first $r+s$ flips to be tails. Thus, the probability all $r+s$ flips are tails is just the probability that the other $s$ flips are all tails. 

$$$$

One could imagine this physically by the following: Imagine your friend flips a coin $r$ times and reports to you that all of them were tails. You then perform $s$ flips on the same coin. The probability that all $r+s$ flips are tails is equal to the probability that you flip $s$ tails. This is the start of your flipping sequence, so the number of flips needed until you obtain a heads is $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$, so the probability that all of the flips you perform are tails is $P(X > s)$. With the specified values, the answer is $8/27$.
hints: To compute this probability, it would know how to compute unconditional probabilities of the form $\prob{X > x}$, where $x$ is an integer. Use the interpretation of the Geometric distribution.

title: Lucky Lottery
statement: A lottery has an urn consisting of $70$ balls labeled distinct numbers $1-70$. $6$ balls are drawn at random for a lottery, and your lottery ticket also has $6$ distinct random numbers $1-70$ on it. You win the lottery if either $5$ or $6$ of your numbers match those drawn (in any order). Find the probability of winning the lottery. If the probability you find is $p$, report $p \cdot 10^6$, rounded to the nearest hundredth.
solution:
Let $N$ be the amount of numbers on the lottery card matching those drawn. We can regard the two groups in this question as numbers matching and numbers not matching those on the lottery card, and $N$ counts the amount of numbers that match. Thus, $N$ must be Hypergeometric, as the numbers are all distinct i.e. selected without replacement.

$$$$

There are $N = 6$ values matching those on your card, $M = 70 - 6 = 64$ values not matching those on your card, and $n = 6$ values selected. Thus $N \sim \text{Hypergeom}(6,64,6)$. To win, you must have at least $5$ numbers match, so the event of winning is the event $\{N \geq 5\} = \{N = 5\}\cup \{N = 6\}$. Since these events are disjoint, $P(N \geq 5) = \mathbb{P}[N = 5] + \mathbb{P}[N = 6]$. By substituting in $N = 6, M = 64, n = 6$, and $k = 5,6$, we obtain 

    $$\mathbb{P}[N = 5] = \dfrac{\displaystyle \binom{6}{5}\binom{64}{1}}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} = \dfrac{384}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} \hspace{3pt} \text{and} \hspace{3pt} \mathbb{P}[N = 6] = \dfrac{\displaystyle \binom{6}{6}\binom{64}{0}}{\displaystyle\binom{70}{6}} = \dfrac{1}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}}$$
Adding these together, the probability of a jackpot is $$P(N \geq 5) = \dfrac{385}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} \approx 2.94 \cdot 10^{-6}$$ The answer is $2.94$.
hints: Let $N$ be the amount of numbers on the lottery card matching those drawn. We can regard the two groups in this question as numbers matching and numbers not matching those on the lottery card, and $N$ counts the amount of numbers that match.
$N$ must be Hypergeometric, as the numbers are all distinct i.e. selected without replacement.

title: Continuous-Time Memorylessness
statement: Let $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $s,t \geq 0$ be fixed real numbers. Compute $\mathbb{P}[X > s + t \mid X > t]$. Report the answer when $\lambda = 1, t = 3,$ and $s = 2$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
For any $x > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}[X > x] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[X \leq x] = 1 - (1-e^{-\lambda x}) = e^{-\lambda x}$$ The first proper step is to apply the definition of conditional probability to the two events. This yields $$\mathbb{P}[X > s + t \mid X > t] = \dfrac{P(X > s+t,X > t)}{P(X > t)} = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[X > s + t]}{\mathbb{P}[X > t]}$$ The numerator event is the intersection of the events $\{X > s+t\}$ and $\{X> t\}$. However, since $s \geq 0$, we have that if $X > s+t$, then $X > t$, so $\{X > s+t$\} a subset of $\{X > t\}$, so the intersection is just $\{X > s+t\}$, justifying the simplification on the numerator. Substituting $x$ as both $s+t$ and $t$ into the expression fro the beginning, $\mathbb{P}[X > s+t] = e^{-\lambda (s+t)}$ and $\mathbb{P}[X > t] = e^{-\lambda t}$. Therefore, $$\mathbb{P}[X > s+t \mid X > t] = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda (s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda t}} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda s} \cdot e^{-\lambda t}}{e^{-\lambda t}} = e^{-\lambda s} = P(X > s)$$ The result of this question is the exact same as in the case of the Geometric distribution, but now for any real $s$ and $t$: $\mathbb{P}[X > s+t \mid X > t] = \mathbb{P}[X > s]$.

$$$$

This result makes intuitive sense by thinking about the meaning of the Exponential distribution. The memorylessness property here says that given you have waited at least $t$ time units for the first occurrence event, the probability you must wait at least $t+s$ time units for the first occurrence of the event is just the probability you must wait $s$ time units (as if it was from the beginning). Imagine the following scenario: You are watching for a certain type of bird, and you wait $t$ units of time for the bird to appear, and it still doesn't. After $t$ units of time, your friend comes in to substitute for you in watching for the bird. The probability that the total time spent watching the bird is at least $t+s$ is therefore just the probability your friend spends at least $s$ units of time watching for the bird. Since the bird hasn't appeared yet, it's as if your friend had started watching from the beginning again, as the state is the exact same. In rough terms, the memorylessness property says: The amount of time that you have already waited for an event to occur does not give any information about how much longer you must wait for an event to occur. With the specified values, the answer is $e^{-2}$.
hints: Complement the CDF and use the definition of conditional probability.

title: Flight Duration III
statement: The length of a flight (in hours) is Exponentially distributed with parameter $1/4$. To the nearest thousandth, find the probability that the flight lasts more than $5$ hours given that it lasts more than $4$ hours.
solution: Using the same notation as the previous parts, $T \sim \exponential{1/4}$ and $F(t) = \left(1 - e^{-t/4}\right)I_{(0,\infty)}(t)$. We want to compute $\mathbb{P}[T > 5 \mid T > 4] = \mathbb{P}[T > 4 + 1 \mid T > 4]$, as we are now given that the flight lasts more than $4$ hours. We write the probability statement in this the form to mimic that of the memorylessness property, as $t = 4$ in this case. By applying the memorylessness of the Exponential distribution and substituting the CDF, $$\mathbb{P}[T > 4 + 1 \mid T > 4] = \mathbb{P}[T > 1] = 1 - P(T \leq 1) = e^{-1/4}$$
hints: Write out the probability statement that you want to compute and apply the memorylessness property of Exponential distributions.

title: Normal Moments I
statement: Suppose that $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Find $E[X^n]$, where $n$ is a positive odd integer. Report the answer when $n = 5$.
solution:
When computing $E[Z^k]$ for a general $k$, computing the $k$th derivative through the MGF or LOTUS explicitly is annoying. However, from the Taylor expansion of the MGF, one can read off the $k$th moment from the coefficient of $\theta^k$. Therefore, the best approach is to consider the Taylor series of the MGF. By taking $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$ in the MGF of the Normal distribution, the MGF of $Z$ is given by $M(\theta) = e^{\frac{1}{2}\theta^2}$. Luckily, we do know the Taylor series of $e^x$, so we can conclude that $$M(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\theta^2\right)^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^k k !}\theta^{2k}$$ Note that there are only even powers of $\theta$ in the Taylor expansion. This means that the coefficient of all odd powers of $\theta$ are $0$, which also means that $E[Z^n] = 0$ when $n$ is odd. Therefore, the answer is $0$.

$$$$

One can also see this result from writing out the LOTUS integral. We have that $$E[Z^n] = \int_{\R} x^n \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}~dx$$ When $n$ is odd, $x^n$ is an odd function. The PDF of the standard Normal distribution is an even function, so their product must be odd. Since their product is odd, we integrate over the entire real line, and MGF exists (implying the integral is finite), we can conclude that the integral must be $0$.
hints: Write out the LOTUS integral or use the MGF of the standard Normal distribution.

title: Carousel Box I
statement: A box has $1$ red and $1$ blue ball. $3$ people named $1,2,$ and $3$, draw from the box one-at-a-time with replacement in that order. A round will be considered as the process of people $1,2,$ and $3$ drawing consecutively. Let $X$ be the number of the person who selects the first red ball and $Y$ be the round in which the first red ball is drawn. For each valid value of $x$ and $y$, compute $P(X = x, Y = y)$. Evaluate this when $x = 1$ and $y = 2$.
solution:
This question is essentially asking us to determine the joint PMF of $X$ and $Y$. Let's first find the joint support. The support of $X$ is $\{1,2,3\}$, as $X$ is just the player number. Now, the support of $Y$ is just $\mathbb{Z}^+$, as any player can win on any round, which are indexed by the positive integers. There is no interaction between the round the player wins on and who is allowed to win, so, the joint support is $S = \{1,2,3\} \times \Z^+$. Thus, for each $x \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, we need to find $\mathbb{P}[X = x, Y = y]$. 

$$$$

The event $\{X = x, Y = y\}$ means that player $x$ must win in round $y$. For this to occur, there can't be a winner in the first $y-1$ rounds, and the people before person $x$ on the $y$th round also can't win. There would be $3(y-1)$ flips that occur in the first $y-1$ rounds, and $x-1$ flips that occur before person $x$ on the $y$th round. Therefore, for this event to occur, the first $3(y-1) + x-1$ draws of the game must all be blue, and then person $x$ must end it with a red. Since each draw is independent, as we draw with replacement, for any $(x,y) \in S$, the probability is given by $$P(X = x, Y = y) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3(y-1) + (x-1)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3(y-1) + x}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/16$.
hints: The support of $X$ is $\{1,2,3\}$, as $X$ is just the player number. Now, the support of $Y$ is just $\mathbb{Z}^+$, as any player can win on any round, which are indexed by the positive integers. There is no interaction between the round the player wins on and who is allowed to win, so, the joint support is $S = \{1,2,3\} \times \Z^+$.
Consider interpreting the event $\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}$ in context of the game.

title: MrBeast's Coin Challenge
statement: You’re pulling up to a MrBeast challenge 🎬, and he hits you with this setup: First, he spins a wheel that randomly picks some probability $X \sim U(0, 1)$. Afterwards, you have to flip a coin with probability $x$ of heads per flip $n$ times, where $n$ is fixed. Let $Y$ be the number of heads that you obtain from your $n$ flips.  As a function of $n$ and/or $y$, for any $0 \leq y \leq n$, compute $P(Y = y)$. Evaluate this when $n = 9$.
solution: This question is really asking us to find the unconditional distribution of $Y$. We must first find the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$. The conditional distribution tells us that for all $y = 0,1,\dots, n$, $$\mathbb{P}[Y = y \mid X = x] = p(y \mid x) = \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}$$ We also have that $f_X(x) = I_{(0,1)}(x)$. By the above work, the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ is $$g(x,y) = p(y \mid x)f_X(x) = \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}I_{(0,1)}(x)$$ To find the unconditional distribution of $Y$, we must remove $X$ from the joint distribution. As $X$ is a continuous random variable, we integrate it out. Note that $Y$ is a discrete random variable, so our result of this integral will be a PMF. Therefore, $$\mathbb{P}[Y = y] = \int_0^1 g(x,y)~dx = \int_0^1 \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}~dx$$ Writing $\displaystyle \binom{n}{y} = \dfrac{n!}{y!(n-y)!}$ and adding and subtracting $1$ from each exponent, we have that the integral becomes $$P(Y = y) = \int_0^1 \dfrac{n!}{y!(n-y)!}x^{\textcolor{red}{(y+1)}-1}(1-x)^{\textcolor{blue}{(n-y+1)}-1}~dx$$ The form of the above integrand suggests that we should transform it into that of a $\bet{\textcolor{red}{y+1}}{\textcolor{blue}{n-y+1}}$ distribution. Note that $y! = \Gamma(y+1)$, $(n-y)! = \Gamma(n-y+1)$, and $n! = \Gamma(n+1)$, which is why we subtracted and added $1$ to each exponent. Writing this in, $$P(Y = y) = \int_0^1 \dfrac{\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(y+1)\Gamma(n-y+1)}x^{(y+1)-1}(1-x)^{(n-y+1)-1}~dx$$ This looks similar to a Beta integral with our desired parameters. However, the normalizing constant is slightly off. The sum of the two parameters of our desired distribution is $n+2$, but the numerator is only $\Gamma(n+1)$. Thus, we must multiply and divide by $n+1$, as we can apply the reduction property $\Gamma(a+1) = a\Gamma(a)$ with $a = n+1$ to get our desired PDF. Our desired integral is therefore $$P(Y = y) = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\int_0^1\dfrac{\Gamma(n+2)}{\Gamma(y+1)\Gamma(n-y+1)}x^{(y+1)-1}(1-x)^{(n-y+1)-1}~dx = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$$ The last integral was that of a PDF, so it evaluates to $1$. The unconditional PMF of $Y$ is given by $\mathbb{P}[Y = y] = 1/(n+1)$ for $y = 0,1,\dots, n$. In other words, $Y \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/10$.
hints: This question is really asking us to find the unconditional distribution of $Y$. We must first find the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$. Afterwards, find the marginal by removing $X$ from the joint. How do you do this?

title: Heads Before Tails
statement: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads is flipped repetitively until $r \geq 1$ heads appear. Find the expected number of tails that appear when $r = 10$ and $p = 1/3$.
solution: As we are waiting for the $r$th occurrence of some events that are independent per trial, we should apply the Negative Binomial distribution. As there is probability $p$ per trial of landing heads and we want $r$ heads, the number of trials needed is $N \sim \negbinom{r}{p}$. From the known properties of the Negative Binomial distribution $E[N] = r/p$. Of these flips, $r$ of them must be heads, so the average number of tails is just the average number of total flips minus the number of heads. Thus, the answer is $$\dfrac{r}{p} - r = r \cdot \dfrac{1-p}{p}$$ This answer passes the intuition check, as $p = 1$ implies that there are no tails, which makes sense, as every flip is a heads. Similarly, if $p = 1/2$, there should intuitively be an equal amount of heads and tails that appear, in which our formula does indeed imply there are $r$ heads and $r$ tails on average. With our specified values, the answer is $20$.
hints: Can you find the total number of flips that it takes on average to obtain $r$ heads? How many of those flips are heads?

title: Limited Hitter I
statement: A standard fair $n-$sided die is rolled infinitely. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls is recorded after each roll. For each integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(n,k)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. For a fixed $k$, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} f(n,k)$. Report the answer when $k = 6$.
solution: As $n \rightarrow \infty$, the number of sides on the die tends to $\infty$. The probability of ever being exactly $k$ must be extremely small as the number of sides grows arbitrarily large. Therefore, it becomes extremely improbable that the sum ever is exactly $k$, as you are extremely likely to exceed $k$ in your first roll! With this intuition in mind, we can conclude that the limit is $0$ for all $k$.
hints: As $n \rightarrow \infty$, the number of sides on the die tends to $\infty$. The probability of ever being exactly $k$ must be extremely small as the number of sides grows arbitrarily large.

title: Both Show
statement: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads is repeatedly flipped until both a heads and tails appear (not necessarily consecutively). Find the expected number of flips that are performed when $p = 1/3$.
solution: Since the two sides are not necessarily equally likely, the expected number of additional flips is dependent on what appears on the first flip. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the first flip. Let $N$ be the total number of flips performed to see both heads and tails. Similarly, let $H$ and $T$ be the events of the first flip being head and tail, respectively. By the Law of Total Expectation, $$E[N] = E[N \mid H]P(H) + E[N \mid T]P(T)$$ As per the question, $P(H) = p$ and $P(T) = 1-p$. If a heads is observed at the first flip, we need to observe a tail. The number of additional flips that need to be performed follows a $\geom{1-p}$ distribution, as there is probability $1-p$ of each flip being tail. The expected number of additional flips needed would be $1/(1-p)$, so $E[N \mid H] = 1 + \frac{1}{1-p}$ The $1$ comes from performing $1$ flip to obtain the initial heads. Similarly, if a tail is observed on the first flip, a head must be seen afterwards. The expected number of additional flips needed in this case is $1/p$, so $E[N \mid T] = 1 + \frac{1}{p}$. Plugging all of these values in yields $$E[T] = p \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{1-p}\right) + (1-p)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{1-p}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{p^2 + (1-p)^2}{p(1-p)} =  \dfrac{1-p(1-p)}{p(1-p)}$$ This expression makes intuitive sense, as it satisfies some properties we would expect. The expected value is minimized at $p = 1/2$, which is reasonable given that the flips are "most random" at $p = 1/2$. Similarly, the expected values grow to $\infty$ as $p \rightarrow 0$ and $p \rightarrow 1$. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $7/2$.
hints: Since the two sides are not necessarily equally likely, the expected number of additional flips is dependent on what appears on the first flip. Use Law of Total Expectation to condition on what happens in the first flip.
What are the distributions of the number of additional flips needed?

title: Absolute Brownian Conditions
statement: Let $W_t$ be a Brownian Motion. For $0 \leq s \leq t$, compute $E[W_s \mid |W_t|]$. Report the answer when $s = 1, t = 3,$ and $|W_t| = 6$.
solution: $|W_t|$ provides us the magnitude, but not direction, of the Brownian Motion. If we knew the direction of the Brownian Motion, we can compute this fairly easily. The idea is to condition on $W_t > 0$ or $W_t \leq 0$ so that we know the direction and magnitude. Applying the Law of Total Expectation, $$E[W_s \mid |W_t|] = E[W_s \mid |W_t|, W_t > 0]P(W_t > 0) + E[W_s \mid |W_t|, W_t \leq 0]P(W_t \leq 0)$$ Since $W_t \sim N(0,t)$, the two probability terms are $0$, as the Normal distribution is symmetric about it's mean. The two conditional expectation terms are now Brownian Bridges on $[0,t]$ that have the same length and opposite direction. The two terms are $\frac{s}{t}|W_t|$ and $-\frac{s}{t}|W_t|$, respectively. Plugging these in, $$E[W_s \mid |W_t|] = \dfrac{s}{t}|W_t| \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{s}{t}|W_t| \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 0$$ This holds for any values of $s,t,$ and $|W_t|$! Intuitively, this makes sense because the Brownian Motion has a density at time $t$ symmetry about $0$, and we only know the magnitude, but not the direction, of the Brownian Motion. Therefore, on average, the process is at $0$ at all times.
hints: $|W_t|$ provides us the magnitude, but not direction, of the Brownian Motion. If we knew the direction of the Brownian Motion, we can compute this fairly easily. The idea is to condition on $W_t > 0$ or $W_t < 0$ so that we know the direction and magnitude.

title: Coin Flipper II
statement: Mike flips a fair coin $n$ times. He starts off with $\$1$. If he receives a heads, he doubles his current balance. If he receives a tails, he loses his entire balance. What is Mike's expected balance at the end? Report the answer when $n = 10$.
solution: If Mike obtains a tails at any point in the $n$ flips, he has $\$0$. Otherwise, if Mike obtains all heads, he has $\$2^n$, as he doubles his money each time. The probability he obtains all heads is $1/2^n$ by independence of the flips. Thus, the probability he obtains at least one tail is $1 - 1/2^n$. By the definition of expected value, Mike's expected balance is $$\dfrac{1}{2^n} \cdot 2^n + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^n}\right) \cdot 0 = 1$$ This is very counter-intuitive, as for any finite $n$, his expected payout is $\$1$, but as $n \rightarrow \infty$, his payout is $\$0$ with probability $1$. This discrepancy arises from deeper measure-theoretic details about the probability space we are working in. In particular, the Dominated Convergence Theorem doesn't apply here. The answer to this question is $\$1$, regardless of $n$.
hints: If Mike obtains a tails at any point in the $n$ flips, he has $\$0$. Otherwise, how much money does he have?

title: Proportional Bets I
statement: George starts with $\$1$. George repeatedly plays a game where he has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning, independently between rounds. If George wins, he receives $\$r$. If George loses, his current balance is multiplied by $0 < q < 1$. If George plays infinitely, what does his expected balance converge to? Report the answer when $p = 1/3, q = 1/2,$ and $r = 3$.
solution: George's wealth after the $(n+1)$st round is dependent on his wealth at the $n$th round. Therefore, the idea is to condition on George's wealth at the $n$th round and derive a recurrence relation to determine his wealth at the $(n+1)$st round. By the Law of Total Expectation, $$E[X_{n+1]} = E[E[X_{n+1] \mid X_n]} = p \cdot (E[X_n] + r) + (1-p)(qE[X_n])$$ The interior was evaluated by conditioning on George winning or losing. If he wins, he obtains $\$r$ extra, which is the first term. Similarly, his balance is multiplied by $q$ if he loses. If we define $E_i = E[X_i]$, we now have a first-order non-homogenous recurrence relation. Suppose that the limit of this relation exists, and call it $L$. Since $L = \displaystyle \lim_{i \rightarrow \infty} E_i = \lim_{i \rightarrow \infty} E_{i-1}$, taking the limit on both sides of the recurrence yields $$L = p(L+r) + (1-p)(qL) \iff L(1-p)(1-q) = pr \iff L = \dfrac{pr}{(1-p)(1-q)}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\$3$.
hints: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be George's wealth after $n$ rounds. To make the notation easier, define $E_i = \ev{X_i}$. Derive a recurrence relation for $E_n$, and then find the limit.

title: Rank and Suit Diff
statement: Two cards are drawn without replacement uniformly at random from a standard deck. Find the probability that the cards differ in both rank and suit.
solution: Since there are the same number of ranks and suits among all different ranks/suits, fix the first card arbitrarily. There are now $51$ cards in the deck remaining. Of these cards, there are $12$ cards from each of the three suits that aren't the one drawn on the first trial that differ in rank as well. Therefore, there are $12 \cdot 3 = 36$ valid cards that can be selected for the second card, so the answer is $36/51 = 12/17$.
hints: Since there are the same number of ranks and suits among all different ranks/suits, fix the first card arbitrarily. How many valid cards remain?

title: Dart Covariance
statement: Maddie is throwing darts at a very realistic dartboard that is infinitely tall and wide. Let $(0,0)$ be the exact center of the bullseye. Let $X$ and $Y$ represent the horizontal and vertical distance that Maddie's dart lands from the bullseye, respectively. This means that Maddie's shot is a random point $(X,Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$. Assume that $X,Y \sim N(0,1)$ IID. Let $R$ be the (Euclidean) distance from the origin that the dart lands. Compute $\text{Cov}(X, R^2)$.
solution: Since $R$ is the distance from the origin, it can be written in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Namely, $R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, so $R^2 = X^2 + Y^2$. We now have a covariance solely in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Substituting in and applying bilinearity, $$\text{Cov}(X, R^2) = \text{Cov}(X, X^2 + Y^2) = \text{Cov}(X, X^2) + \text{Cov}(X, Y^2)$$ Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, the second covariance is $0$. To compute the first covariance, we can expand it out with the common formula to obtain $$\text{Cov}(X, X^2) = E[X^3] - E[X]E[X^2]$$ Recall that all odd moments of the standard Normal distribution are $0$, so the above term also vanishes. Therefore, $\text{Cov}(X, R^2) = 0$.
hints: Since $R$ is the distance from the origin, it can be written in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Substitute that into the covariance and use bilinearity.

title: Correlated Indicators
statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be events with $0 < P(A), P(B) < 1$. Define $I_A$ and $I_B$ to be the indicator random variables of $A$ and $B$, respectively. Suppose $\text{Corr}(I_A, I_B) = \rho$. If possible, find $\text{Corr}(I_{A^c)}{I_{B^c}}$ when $\rho = 0.3$. If not, answer $-2$.
solution: Let's first understand how the indicator of an event and it's complement are related. $I_A = 1$ exactly when $A$ occurs, which means $I_{A^c} = 0$. Similarly, $I_A = 0$ exactly when $A$ doesn't occur i.e. $A^c$ occurs, so $I_{A^c} = 1$. We can encapsulate this relationship by saying $I_{A^c} = 1 - I_A$. The same idea holds for $B$. Therefore, $$\text{Corr}(I_{A^c)}{I_{B^c}} = \text{Corr}(1 - I_A, 1 - I_B)$$ This is a linear transformation of the original indicators. From the properties of correlation, for any real constants $a,b,c,$ and $d$, with $a,c \neq 0$, $\text{Corr}(aX+b, cY+d) = \text{sign}(ac)\text{Corr}(X, Y)$, as the magnitude of the correlation is unchanged. In this case, $a = c = -1$, while $b = d = 1$. Therefore, $\text{sign}(ac) = \text{sign}(1) = 1$, meaning $\text{Corr}(I_A, I_B) = \text{Corr}(I_{A^c)}{I_{B^c}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $0.3$.
hints: $I_A = 1$ exactly when $I_{A^c} = 0$, and vice versa. Therefore, for any event $E$, $I_E = 1 - I_{E^c}$. What do you know about correlation and linear transformations?

title: Dying Population
statement: Consider a population that originally consists of $N$ individuals. Each individual dies independently of one another, and the time of the last death has no bearing on when the next death occurs. When there are exactly $i$ individuals in the population, the rate of death of each individual in the population is $\mu_i$. Find the expected amount of time until the population goes extinct when $N = 4$ and $\mu_i = \frac{1}{5-i}$.
solution: The death rate is constant given the amount of people in the population, so it's best to break up the problem into distinct time intervals based on the population: Time spent with $N$ individuals, $N-1$ individuals, and so on. Let $T_i$ be the amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals in the population. The total lifetime of the population is given by $T = T_N + T_{N-1} + \dots + T_1$. The sum stops at $1$ because $T_1$ is the amount of time spent until the last individual dies, in which extinction is reached. The random variables are not exchangeable, as they don't have the same death rates. Applying linearity of expectation, $$E[T] = \sum_{i=1}^N E[T_i]$$ $\mathbb{E}[T_i]$ is the expected time spent with exactly $i$ individuals. Each individual dies independently of each other and with respect to when the last individual died. Thus, the rate of death when there are exactly $i$ individuals must be $i\mu_i$, as each individual dies at a rate $\mu_i$ and there are $i$ independent individuals in the population. Since the rate of death is $i\mu_i$ per unit time, the expected amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals is $E[T_i] = \frac{1}{i\mu_i}$. Substituting in, $$E[T] = \sum_{i=1}^N = \dfrac{1}{i\mu_i}$$ With the specified values, $E[T] = 77/12$.
hints: The death rate is constant given the amount of people in the population, so it's best to break up the problem into distinct time intervals based on the population: Time spent with $N$ individuals, $N-1$ individuals, and so on. Let $T_i$ be the amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals in the population. Use linearity of expectation somehow.

title: Linearly Normal I
statement: Suppose $X,Y \sim N(0,1)$ IID. For any constants $a,b > 0$, compute $E[aX + bY \mid X+Y]$. Report your answer when $a = 2, b = 4,$ and $X+Y = 2$.
solution: Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, we obtain some symmetry that simplifies the problem. In particular, as $X$ and $Y$ are IID and the given information is symmetric in $X$ and $Y$, $E[X \mid X+Y] = E[Y \mid X+Y]$. By the linearity of conditional expectation and known information, $$E[X \mid X+Y] + E[Y \mid X+Y] = E[X+Y \mid X+Y] = X+Y$$ By the equality above, $$E[X \mid X +Y ] = E[Y \mid X+Y] = \dfrac{X+Y}{2}$$ This intuitively makes sense, as each should contribute equally to the sum $X+Y$ on average since they are IID. With this information in hand, we can apply linearity of conditional expectation to our original problem and obtain $$E[aX + bY \mid X+Y] = aE[X \mid X+Y] + bE[Y \mid X+Y] = (X+Y) \cdot \dfrac{a+b}{2}$$ Plugging in the specified values, the answer is $6$.
hints: Apply linearity of conditional expectation. Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, what can be said about the conditional expectation term?

title: Zeta Zonk I
statement: We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. For positive integers $k$, define $D_k$ to be the event that $p_k$ divides $X$. Find $P(D_k)$ when $k = 4$ and $s = 3$.
solution: For $p_k \mid X$, $X$ must be an integer multiple of $p_k$. In other words, $X = np_k$ for some positive integer $k$. The events $\{X = np_k\}$ are disjoint for varying $n$, so we can say $$P(D_k) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} P(X = np_k) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(np_k)^{-s}}{\zeta(s)} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s \cdot \zeta(s)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^s} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s}$$ The last term was evaluated by the definition of $\zeta(s)$. With the specified values, $p_4 = 7$, so the answer is $1/343$.
hints: For $p_k \mid X$, $X$ must be an integer multiple of $p_k$. In other words, $X = np_k$ for some positive integer $k$. The events $\{X = np_k\}$ are disjoint for varying $n$.

title: Void Suits
statement: A casino deals deals you $13$ cards from a standard deck of $52$ cards. We say that a hand is void of a suit if it has no cards from that suit. Compute the probability that you are void in at least one suit. Round your answer the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let's first frame this problem with events. First, arbitrarily label the suits $1-4$. This can be done because all suits have the same number of cards. For $k = 1,2,3,4$, let $A_k$ be the event that you are void in suit $k$. More simply stated, $A_k$ is the event that your hand has no card from suit $k$. The event
of being void in at least one suit is now $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup A_4$. We choose unions since it is an "at least" problem. Note that the events $A_1,\dots, A_4$ depend on one another: For example, the hand is void of three suits, it can't be void of the last suit. Therefore, complementation doesn't work. Instead, we apply the inclusion-exclusion formula. The probability of being void in a suit shouldn't depend on what the suit or suits we're void in, so the second special case of the inclusion-exclusion formula holds. 

$$$$

To compute the probabilities, consider the interpretation of each event. For example, for $A_1$ to occur, no cards from suit $1$ can be selected. Thus, $13$ cards must be selected from the other $52-13 = 39$ cards that are not of suit $1$, which can be done in $\binom{39}{13}$ ways. There are $\binom{52}{13}$ ways to pick $13$ cards with no restrictions. Similarly, for $A_1 \cap A_2$ to occur, the $13$ cards must come from the other $26$ cards that are of suits $3$ or $4$. Applying this logic yields 
$$\mathbb{P}[A_1] = \frac {{39\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}}, \quad \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2] = \frac {{26\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}},$$
$$\mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3] = \frac {{13\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}},\quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3\cap A_4]=0$$

$$$$

We can now apply the inclusion-exclusion formula directly.
$$P(\bigcup_{k=1)^4 A_k} = \binom{4}{1}\mathbb{P}[A_1] - \binom{4}{2} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2] +
\binom{4}{3} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2 \cap A_3] - \binom{4}{4} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3 \cap A_4]$$
$$=4\cdot \frac {{39\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} - 6\cdot 
\frac {{26\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} + 4\cdot \frac {{13\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} \approx 0.051$$
hints:
Let's first frame this problem with events. First, arbitrarily label the suits $1-4$. This can be done because all suits have the same number of cards. For $k = 1,2,3,4$, let $A_k$ be the event that you are void in suit $k$. More simply stated, $A_k$ is the event that your hand has no card from suit $k$. The event
of being void in at least one suit is now $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup A_4$. We choose unions since it is an "at least" problem. Note that the events $A_1,\dots, A_4$ depend on one another.

title: Big Up Chip
statement: A box has $n$ chips labeled with distinct numbers $1$ to $n$. You draw two chips at random without replacement and record their values. Find the probability that the larger of the two values is exactly $1 \leq k \leq n-1$ larger than the smaller of the two values. Evaluate this when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution: Since each pair of values is equally likely to be selected, we can compute the probability by counting. There are $\binom{n}{2}$ ways to pick two distinct chips. To have a difference of exactly $k$ between the chips, the chip values must be in the form $(i,i+k)$ for some value $i$. The possible values of $i$ are $1 \leq i \leq n-k$ to ensure that both bounds are within $\{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Therefore, the probability of selecting two chips with difference exactly $k$ is $$\dfrac{n-k}{\binom{n}{2}} = \dfrac{2(n-k)}{n(n-1)}$$With the specified values, the answer is $2/15$.
hints: To have a difference of exactly $k$ between the chips, the chip values must be in the form $(i,i+k)$ for some value $i$.

title: All and None
statement: Let $S$ be a set of $2^n$ elements. Suppose that $A_1,\dots, A_n$ are subsets of $S$ selected independently and uniformly at random from all $2^{2^n}$ subsets of $S$. Define $p(n)$ to be the probability that $\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i = S$ and $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i = \emptyset$. If it exists, determine $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p(n)$ to the nearest thousandth. If this limit does not exist, report the answer $-1$.
solution:
To evaluate the limit, we should evaluate $p(n)$ for fixed $n$ first. For each $s \in S$, we want it to be in at least one of the sets $A_1,\dots, A_n$, but not all of them. Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, there is probability $1/2$ for each $s \in S$ of it being in $A_i$ or not in $A_i$ for all $i$.

$$$$

To compute the probability above for a singular $s \in S$, we should consider the complement, as we are looking at an "at least one" probability. The complement of being in at least one but not all is $s$ belongs to either none or all of $A_1,\dots, A_n$. By independence of the selected sets, the probability $s$ belongs to none of the $A_i$ sets is $1/2^n$. Similarly, the probability $s$ beongs to all of the $A_i$ sets is $1/2^n$. Thus, with probability $1 - (1/2^n + 1/2^n) = 1 - 1/2^{n-1}$, $s$ belongs to at least one and not all of $A_1,\dots, A_n$. Note that there are $2^n$ total elements in $S$. The decision of which of the $A_i$ sets a fixed $s$ belongs to is independent between elements. Therefore, the probability that this condition holds for all of the elements is given by $$p(n) = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right)^{2^n}$$ This limit looks similar to that of the definition of $e$. To evaluate this limit, we can apply the following lemma: If $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ are two sequences of real numbers such that $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = 0$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_nb_n = c$, then $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(1 + a_n\right)^{b_n} = e^c$. This can be proved using the tools of an introductory calculus course. In this case, $a_n = -1/2^{n-1}$ and $b_n = 2^n$. These sequences satisfy the conditions, and $a_nb_n = -2$ for all $n$, meaning the limit is also $-2$. Therefore, $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p(n) = e^{-2}$.
hints: To evaluate the limit, we should evaluate $p(n)$ for fixed $n$ first. For each $s \in S$, we want it to be in at least one of the sets $A_1,\dots, A_n$, but not all of them. Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, there is probability $1/2$ for each $s \in S$ of it being in $A_i$ or not in $A_i$ for all $i$.

title: One Then Two
statement: Two fair standard $n-$sided dice are rolled until at least one $1$ appears. Upon stopping, find the probability that both dice show $1$ when $n = 8$.
solution: Since the dice are fair, we can convert this into a counting problem. The number of outcomes where both dice show $1$ is clearly $1$. To count the number of outcomes where at least one die shows the value $1$, we can apply complementation. This works because we are looking to count an "at least one" event. The complement of having at least one $1$ appear is having no $1$s appear. There are $n^2$ total outcomes without restrictions. If neither die is a $1$, then there are $n-1$ outcomes per die, so there are $(n-1)^2$ total outcomes without a $1$. Thus, $n^2 - (n-1)^2 = 2n-1$ outcomes have at least one $1$. Therefore, the probability is $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $1/15$.
hints: How many outcomes have at least one $1$ appearing? How many have both ones appearing?

title: Nearest Diagonal I
statement: A point is selected uniformly at random from the unit square. Find the expected distance of the point to the $y = x$ line to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let $D$ be the distance to the $y=x$ line. We don't know the PDF of $D$ directly, which makes direct integration not possible. Instead, we can consider the tail integral formula $E[X] = \ctailsum{X}$. This is the best way because we don't know the PDF nor any direct symmetry in this scenario.

$$$$

In this scenario, we are looking at the perpendicular distance from the points to the diagonal. Thus, the maximum possible distance to the $y=x$ line occurs at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$, which are both $1/\sqrt{2}$ distance away from the $y=x$ line, as the nearest point is $(1/2,1/2)$. To find the distance of a point $(x,y)$ from the line $ax + by + c = 0$, we can use the distance formula $$d(ax+by+c=0, (x,y)) = \dfrac{|ax + by + c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$$ In this case, $y = x$ can be written as $x-y = 0$, so the distance of a point $(x,y)$ to the line is given by $|x-y|/\sqrt{2}$. We can now express $D = |X-Y|/\sqrt{2}$. Using this, $$\{D \geq d\} = \left\{\dfrac{|X-Y|}{\sqrt{2}} \geq d\right\} = \{|X-Y| \geq d\sqrt{2}\}$$ Drawing this region out in the plane, we get two disjoint right triangles whose side lengths are $1-d\sqrt{2}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform, we can take a ratio of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the full support is $1$, while the area of the two triangles is given by $2 \cdot 1/2 (1-d\sqrt{2})^2 = (1-d\sqrt{2})^2$. Thus, $P(D \geq d) = (1-d\sqrt{2})^2$. Plugging this into the continuous tail integral formula yields $$E[D] = \int_0^{1/\sqrt{2}} (1-x\sqrt{2})^2~dx = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}$$
hints: Let $D$ be the distance to the $y=x$ line. Consider the continuous tail expectation formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. What does the event $\{D \geq d\}$ look like, and what are the bounds on it?

title: Convolution Convergence I
statement: Let $X$ be a random variable with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Fix $0 < \lambda < 1$, and define the sequence of random variables as follows, where $'$ denotes an independent copy of the random variable: $Y_1 = \lambda X + (1-\lambda)X'$ and $Y_{n+1} = \lambda Y_n + (1-\lambda) Y_n'$. If it exists, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} E[Y_n]$ when $\lambda = 1/3, \mu = 4,$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$. If the limit does not exist, enter $-100$.
solution: Since we know how to express $Y_n$ in terms of $Y_{n-1}$, we should relate the two expected values. By linearity of expectation, $$E[Y_n] = E[\lambda Y_{n-1] + (1-\lambda) Y_{n-1}'} = \lambda E[Y_{n-1]} + (1-\lambda)E[Y_{n-1]'} = E[Y_{n-1]}$$ The expected values combine because $Y_{n-1}$ and $Y_{n-1}'$ are IID. Therefore, $E[Y_n] = E[Y_1]$ for all $n$, and we know $$E[Y_1] = E[\lambda X + (1-\lambda) X'] = \lambda E[X] + (1-\lambda)E[X'] = E[X] = \mu$$ Therefore, the answer is $\mu$, as all terms in the sequence are $\mu$. The answer for the specified values given here is $4$.
hints: Can you find $\ev{Y_n}$ for general $n$ by linearity of expectation? You can express $Y_n$ in terms of $Y_{n-1}$.

title: Variable Gambler
statement: You got to Vegas successfully. They call you the variable gambler. You play a slot machine such that you win with probability $1/2$ your first turn. After the first turn, you win with probability $1/2$ if you lost the previous turn and with probability $0 < p < 1/2$ if you won the previous turn. Let $p_n$ be the probability that you win on the $n$th turn. Evaluate $p_4$ when $p = 1/3$.
solution:
The probability that you win on your current turn is dependent on whether you won or lost in the previous turn. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on whether you won or lost on the previous turn. If you won on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $p_{n-1}$, then you win with probability $p$ on this turn. Otherwise, if you lost on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $1-p_{n-1}$, you win on this turn with probability $1/2$. Applying the Law of Total Probability, we get $$p_n = pp_{n-1} + (1-p_{n-1})\cdot 1/2 \iff p_n = (p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2$$ To solve this recurrence, the best method is by differencing, as it has a constant of $1/2$ out back. This allows us to eliminate the constant. Since we will get to a term with $p_1$ in it, it helps to define $p_1 = 1/2$, which is consistent with the information in the question. We will derive a recurrence for $r_n = p_n - p_{n-1}$. Namely, $$p_n - p_{n-1} = \left[(p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2\right] - \left[(p - 1/2)p_{n-2} + 1/2\right] = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2})$$ This is now a fairly easy recurrence to solve. Namely, we get that $$p_n - p_{n-1} = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2}) = (p-1/2)^2(p_{n-2} - p_{n-3}) = \dots = (p-1/2)^{n-2}(p_{2} - p_{1})$$ Recall that $p_1 = 1/2$ from the above. We can use the recurrence to obtain $p_2 = 1/2 \cdot p + 1/2 \cdot 1/2 = (2p+1)/4$, so $p_2 - p_1 = (2p-1)/4$. We now have a simple recurrence to solve, since the term out back is summable. Namely,
\begin{align*}
    p_n &= p_{n-1} + \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\\
    &= p_{n-2} +  \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot\left[ \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-3} + \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\right]\\
    &= \dots \\
    &= p_1 + \dfrac{2p-1}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{n-2} \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{k}\\
    &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{1-(p-1/2)^{n-1}}{1-(p-1/2)}\\
    &=\dfrac{1-(p-1/2)^n}{3-2p}
\end{align*}

$$$$

The geometric series formula was used with common ratio $p - 1/2$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{185}{432}$.
hints: The probability that you win on your current turn is dependent on whether you won or lost the previous turn. Condition on whether you won or lost on the previous turn.

title: Arc Up I
statement: Two points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of a semi-circle of radius $1$, including the diameter at the bottom. Find the probability that exactly one point lies on the diameter to the nearest thousandth.
solution: The length of the diameter is $2$, while the length of the circular portion is $\pi$. Thus, the total length is $2 + \pi$. By the uniformity of the selection, the probability that any given point lands on the diameter is $\frac{2}{2 + \pi}$, while the probability it lands on the circular portion is $\frac{\pi}{2+\pi}$. There are $2$ ways to arrange the points between the portions (first one diameter and second circular, or vice-versa). By independence of the points, the probability of exactly one point in each region is $$2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{2 + \pi} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2 + \pi} = \dfrac{4\pi}{(2+\pi)^2} \approx 0.475$$
hints: What is the total length of the perimeter of the circle, including the diameter?

title: Lotto I
statement: Let $N > 0$ be fixed. $2N$ people play the lottery each week. Each of the people are assigned a uniformly random integer in $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, independently of other people. One of the $N$ integers is selected uniformly at random to be the winning value. Let $W_N$ be the random variable that counts the number of people that win the lottery in a given week. Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} P(W_N \leq 3)$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: For a fixed $N$, $W_N$ counts the number of successes in $2N$ independent trials (people). The success probability is $1/N$, as one of the $N$ values is the correct one. Therefore, $W_N \sim \text{Bin}(2N, 1/N)$. Note that as $N \rightarrow \infty$, the success probability is tending to $0$. Since we have a limit of Binomial random variables that have trials tending to $\infty$ and success probabilities tending to $0$, we should consider the Poisson limit theorem. The means of the Binomial distributions converge to $2$. Therefore, by the Poisson limit theorem, $\displaystyle \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} P(W_N \leq 3) = P(X \leq 3)$, where $X \sim \poisson{2}$. Using the PMF of $X$, $$P(X \leq 3) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) + P(X = 3) = \dfrac{19}{3e^2}$$
hints: For a fixed $N$, what is the distribution of $W_N$? Can you use some limit theorem here?

title: Die Duo I
statement: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. While your die is a standard fair $6-$sided die, your friend's die has the values $111666$ on the sides. Both of you roll the die one time. Find the probability that you roll a strictly higher value than your friend.
solution: To roll strictly higher than your friend, they must obtain a $1$ on their die, as it's not possible for your to obtain a strictly larger value than $6$. Your friend rolls $1$ with probability $1/2$. Given your friend rolls a $1$, you must obtain some value strictly larger than $1$. This occurs with probability $5/6$ on your die, as all outcomes but $1$ are strictly better than your friend's roll. Therefore, the answer is $5/6 \cdot 1/2 = 5/12$.
hints: Is it possible to roll strictly higher if your friend obtains a $6$?

title: Container Circle I
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the unit circle. Find the expected area of the largest circle centered at the origin that contains no points when $n = 4$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The largest circle that doesn't contain any points would have a radius equal to the minimum distance of any points from the origin. Thus, the area of this circle is $A = \pi R^2$, where $R = \min\{R_1,\dots, R_n\}$ and $R_1,\dots, R_n$ are the IID distances of the selected points from the origin. The maximum possible area of the circle is $\pi$, as that would be the entire region itself. Therefore, we integrate on $(0,\pi)$ and obtain $$E[A] = \int_0^{\pi} P(A \geq x)~dx = \int_0^{\pi} P(\pi R^2 \geq x)~dx = \int_0^{\pi} P(R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x){\pi}}}~dx$$ The event $\left\{R \geq \sqrt{\frac{x}{\pi}}\right\}$ means that no point lies within a distance of $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ of the origin. Since the points are selected uniformly at random, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the region more than $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is $\pi\left(1 - (\sqrt{x/\pi})^2\right)$, as the collection of points whose distance is at most $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is a circle of radius $\sqrt{x/\pi}$. We used the complement to compute the area. The total area of the region is $\pi$, so the probability of any given point being a distance more than $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ away from the origin is $1 - x/\pi$ by dividing. Since there are $n$ independently selected points that all must satisfy this condition to ensure the minimum distance is at least $\sqrt{x/\pi}$, $$P(A \geq x)  = P(R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x){\pi}}} = \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n$$ Plugging this into the integral with the $u-$substitution $u = x/\pi$, we get $$E[A] = \int_0^{\pi} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n~dx = \pi \int_0^1 (1-u)^n ~du = \dfrac{\pi}{n+1}$$ With $n = 4$, the answer is $\pi/5$.
hints: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The largest circle that doesn't contain any points would have a radius equal to the minimum distance of any points from the origin.

title: Container Square II
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the square centered at the origin with vertices at $(\pm 1,\pm 1)$. Find the expected area of the smallest square centered at the origin that contains all $n$ points when $n = 9$.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the square. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and side length are related.
